items.title: Nike’s new air sole technology can mix soft and firm cushioning
paragraphs: is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

In 2024, Nike announced its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The company is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using its new Tuned Air technology. While previously the level of cushioning in Nike Air shoes was uniform across the entire sole, a new manufacturing process can produce multiple air pockets with varying levels of cushioning and stability.

Nike has been putting air pockets into its shoes for nearly 50 years as a way to increase comfort and cushioning while making them lighter. Its air pockets have even found their way into apparel as a way to improve insulation by trapping body heat, but Nike plans to use its new Tuned Air technology as a way to customize the cushioning experience in its shoes and tailor them to specific athletes and sports. The first shoes featuring the technology are expected to arrive in late 2027 and will be targeted at runners.

While one of Nike’s earliest successes was track shoes with a grip design inspired by a waffle iron, the company credits the “vibrant colors on magazine covers” as the inspiration for its latest shoe technology. A Tuned Air sole is manufactured using a “proprietary digital print and selective lamination process” where an ink is applied in specific patterns that define where the layers bond to each other. This process can be used to create internal pockets in an unlimited combination of shapes and sizes, and by fine-tuning how much air is in each of those pockets, some parts of the sole can feel firmer while others feel softer.

The Tuned Air technology will not only allow Nike to highly customize the fit and feel of air sole shoes for different sports, it will also help keep the benefits of the custom tuning consistent across different sizes. The new manufacturing process will also help reduce the amount of time it takes Nike to go from a concept for a new shoe to a final design ready for production. “Prototypes that once took three weeks can now be made in three days,” the company claims in a release today. That gives Nike’s designers more time to refine new shoes, and more opportunity to experiment.

items.title: ‘Heads should roll’: owner of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in skip bin demands probe
paragraphs: So You Are’s owner-breeder has demanded a full investigation after the Melbourne Cup runner’s body was found in a skip at a Sydney tip, insisting “heads have got to roll”.
Stuart Ramsey says it is a “bloody disgrace” the gelding was left in the skip bin while awaiting burial at Sydney’s Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre.
The grisly sight was uncovered by a Sydney man, with online footage outraging industry participants and anti-horse racing activists alike.
Bjorn Baker’s promising stayer took ill at a spelling farm after finishing eighth in Australia’s most famous race on 3 November.

He was rushed to the REC Equine Specialists veterinary clinic at Horsley Park in Sydney’s west after showing signs of colic on Monday morning. Surgery could not save the horse and he was euthanised under anaesthesia.
Racing NSW said its ongoing investigations found So You Are was being held temporarily awaiting burial when the footage was recorded.

While REC has apologised, Ramsey, a renowned breeder at boutique Hunter Valley farm Turangga Stud, wants answers and accountability over the disposal of the five-year-old, who earned A$1.4m from eight career wins.
“There should be a full investigation. Heads have got to roll – simple as that,” Ramsey said.
“He was more than just a racehorse. He brought our family together, and to think of the stress the family are under now because of this – it’s a bloody disgrace.
“We took 30-odd people down to Melbourne for the race. So You Are brought us all together, as only a horse can do. It’s very sad that it’s happened.”

REC’s managing partner, Jonathan Lumsden, said the centre had spoken with So You Are’s owners and trainers to apologise. He said the veterinary practice did not carry out the burial, but took “full responsibility” for choosing the service provider and arrangements.
“He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” Lumsden said in a statement.
Ramsey, who said he had not been contacted by REC, said he is not satisfied with their explanation.
“So they should take responsibility. It wasn’t the contractor’s fault; it was their fault. They were in charge of the horse,” he said.
“They didn’t even give us the option of burying him up at Turangga ... they should all be out – gone. I don’t mean everyone, but the bosses and the people who’ve made the decisions.”
Ramsey declared racehorses are among the best looked-after animals in the world and spoke of his affinity for So You Are. “He meant so much to us,” he said.
The treatment of So You Are’s remains has sparked strong criticism from animal welfare groups.
“There is always the option to bury the horse or have the horse cremated,” Elio Celotto, the campaign director for the Coalition for the Protection of Racehorses, said.
“However, it is more expedient to dump the horse at a local tip. This is business as usual for an industry where profit is always more important than sentiment.”
Georgie Purcell, a Victorian Animal Justice Party MP, said the tragic case should force the industry to confront serious questions about duty of care.
“The racing industry breeds these horses and profits from them but fails the most basic obligation to treat them with dignity after death,” she said.
Racing NSW said “appropriate action” would be taken if any wrongdoing was discovered in its ongoing investigation .
“Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process,” it said.
“That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.”
Baker said he was also left deeply distressed by the handling of the much-loved horse’s remains, adding they deserved to be treated with dignity and respect.

items.title: Russian military plane crashes killing all 19 on board
paragraphs: A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.

CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

items.title: Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
paragraphs: Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives.

Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.

Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents.

Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.

Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram.

Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

items.title: Campaigners take claim 'regulatory gap' risks poultry farms polluting rivers to High Court
paragraphs: The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital".
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
The three farms are Neuadd Isaf, Rhosddu and Llanshay.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved last year.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

items.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
paragraphs: An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.

“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.

The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.

The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.

“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.

Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”

items.title: Instagram is helping creators crack down on copycat videos
paragraphs: is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Instagram is beginning to roll out a “content protection” feature that lets creators see and review copies of their videos posted to the platform.

“For eligible creators who enroll, content protection is a tool that automatically looks out for visual matches of your original videos, alerts you when we find a match across Instagram and Facebook, and lets you decide what happens next,” Meta says in a blog post. Meta launched a similar tool for Facebook last year to help users “safeguard” their Reels and “maintain control” over their creative work.

When an Instagram creator is notified of a matched video, they can see how many views the match has and decide if they want to track the video, hide it from everyone on Instagram and Facebook, add a credit link, or release their claim on the match.

After a creator enrolls, every “original video” they post on Instagram is protected, and creators can retroactively protect older videos manually. Creators can also put accounts on an allow list that lets them use their videos.

In addition, Instagram will start flagging AI-generated videos that “match the spoken words” in a creator’s original video but have visuals replaced with AI. Initially, Instagram will test this with a “small group of creators” in “the coming weeks.” The platform says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that “use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly.”

items.title: University pauses Shakespeare move after backlash
paragraphs: The university said it would work with the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, institute staff, students, alumni and other partners over the coming months.
Tickell said the university's commitment to Shakespearean studies had "never been in doubt" but added that interest in studying in Stratford had remained low for several years.

He said related subjects had seen significant growth on the university's Birmingham campus, while the city's creative industries sector offered opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.

"Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students, and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England's greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Liberal Democrat MP Perteghella described the proposed move as "ill-thought" and "shocking".
She said she would raise the issue in Parliament and write to the university about her "deep disappointment" and concerns for the institute's future.

items.title: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
paragraphs: A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who has served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

items.title: Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave
paragraphs: On a harried Saturday afternoon at Denver International Airport, I had the good fortune of sitting just a few feet from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise. He, I, and 3,500 or so others had just left “What’s Next,” a conference organized by Majority Democrats, a group dedicated to charting a path for the suddenly — and shockingly? — victorious party.

Frey, who rose to national prominence amid ICE’s brutal Operation Metro Surge, had come to the conference in Denver to listen, not to speak. “I’ve never been to one of these things before,” he said. He had flown in for a day and, like everyone else in attendance, is curious to see where the party goes from here. He said he hopes Democrats do two things with their newfound power. “One, act with urgency. And second, don’t fuck it up.”
Another conference-goer sitting nearby chimed in: “Abso-fucking-lutely.”

Democrats, unaccustomed to winning, have seemingly learned from the folly of Republicans’ 2024 sweep. Where Donald Trump’s return to power was falsely attributed to a vibe shift of seismic proportions, born of voters’ preoccupation over DEI and desire to say slurs, Majority Democrats has a simpler explanation for the blue tsunami: It’s the economy, stupid. Everything is falling apart, and even just getting by feels more expensive than ever. The midterms were a rejection, not an endorsement: Voters rejected data centers, they rejected war, and they cast their lot with the side that promised to give them what they want.

The Democrats understand this is not a cultural victory. Even the hollow center of the Democratic Party has, at long last, realized voters don’t necessarily want what they’re selling — they just want to afford to live. It’s gas and groceries all the way down. This analysis would almost verge on Marxist if it wasn’t put forth by an organization comprising the party’s new, young moderates. Majority Democrats describes itself as an alternative to three unpopular, ineffective factions: the “gerontocratic establishment,” the “activist left,” and the “MAGA right.”

The Democrats want you to know they’ve changed. This is no longer the party of “Kamala is brat” or “Pokémon Go to the polls.” They are, in fact, “A Different Kind of Democrat.” They’ve abandoned hollow identity politics and sworn off toxic factional infighting. They really, really care about affordability — for real. They even have the merch to prove it.

Attendees at What’s Next wore their convictions on their sleeves, and also their chests, and also their heads. There were hats that read “pay your taxes” and hats identifying the wearer as a “new deal democrat,” both in all lowercase because the Democrats would also like to remind you that they are once again the youth party. At a separate merch stand, there was a T-shirt declaring “America!” and another T-shirt posing an existential question, also in all lowercase: “how did fucking computers become the thing and machines became the thing that does art? and humans are like the ones in amazon warehouses like shouldn’t robots be working so we can paint?” This second shirt, a friend pointed out, is an uncredited reference to a joke alt-comedian Stavros Halkias made on Theo Von’s podcast. And there was the Our Get Along Shirt, a sartorial exercise in magical thinking that summed up the ethos of the What’s Next conference. The Democrats were in control. Having realized the folly of fighting each other, they would instead channel their energy into fighting for the American people.

The illusion of harmony was shattered early into the programming when a small group of dissenters heckled Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the soon-to-be speaker of the House. “We’re asking you to listen to us now,” one of the protesters shouted after the moderator, Fox News’s resident Democratic host Jessica Tarlov, attempted to placate them by saying she’d be asking Jeffries about the youth vote. “When is the time for a Green New Deal? When is the time for an arms embargo?” The protesters’ cries were drowned out by the crowd’s chants of “HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM.”

Jeffries, ever the politician, was unfazed by the altercation. “I’m from Brooklyn,” he told his visibly uncomfortable interlocutor. “This is light work.” The protesters were whisked away, and the interview continued as if the interruption had never happened. Democrats would be gracious in victory.

This new way of doing things was best summed up by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who told reporters that she and her new colleague, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, had plenty of debates in the car en route to campaign events — though she declined to say what the debates were about. (Slotkin has identified as a Zionist but has also voted against providing certain military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has called Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide.) “Abdul and I do not agree on everything, but we agree on the really big, important thing, and that is making sure we have a middle class in this country,” she said. “When I see elected officials spending their time fighting the progressive-versus-moderate battle, I know that person didn’t actually learn a damn thing from the election.”

Throughout the weekend, speaker after speaker urged Democrats not to squander their newfound control of Congress by bickering among themselves. At the airport, notorious Democratic operative Lis Smith, an adviser to Majority Democrats, told me the midterms sweep was a rejection of Trumpism, not a sign that voters prefer one style of Democratic politics over the other. “A big takeaway of the election was that there’s no one way to be a Democrat, and that’s in part how we were able to have such a big victory,” she said. The calls for unity were reminiscent of the slogan of one doomed 2016 presidential campaign: Stronger Together. This time, however, they may be onto something — at least for now.

“It’s easy to have Pete Buttigieg and Ro Khanna onstage when we’re all riding the same high,” one staffer told me on the final night of the conference. But what happens when it’s actually time to govern?
For all the talk of unity, there was plenty of tension at What’s Next — sometimes overt, more often simmering beneath the surface of what organizers described as a congenial event.

There was tension toward the establishment, as characterized by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s announcement that he was challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for Senate majority leader. There was tension between speakers’ repeated exhortations to get “big money” out of politics and the fact that Majority Democrats is largely bankrolled by hedge fund billionaire Stephen Mandel, a major investor in companies powering the AI boom. (Several attendees I spoke to described What’s Next as hands down the most luxe Democratic event they’ve been to, on par with the party’s national conventions. The snack station was stocked with full-size candy bars.) There was tension between all the populist posturing and the nightly afterparties at the Ritz, where 2028 contenders, staffers, and hangers-on of all types drank well after last call. And notwithstanding the recent blue tsunami, there was tension between Democrats’ persistent unlikability and the conference’s poptimism-tinged branding.

Everything was a little too cute. Majority Democrats staffers wore custom Dickies-style jackets with their names embroidered on the front. Highlight reels played between each main stage speech. The opening-night happy hour, sponsored by the Searchlight Institute — a think tank founded in 2025 with the stated goal of weakening the influence of liberal groups like the ACLU and the Center for American Progress — was Western-themed, though hardly any attendees strayed from the blazer-and-lanyard dress code that is de rigueur in liberal policy circles. The conference lineup was announced via a music festival-style flyer. The halls were decorated with stylized posters of the politicians in attendance, many of whom seemed to be soft-launching their 2028 presidential campaigns.

“The organizers here want a big tent — one big enough even to invite anti-establishment voices like me,” Khanna, one apparent presidential aspirant, said from the stage. “I’m all for a big tent. I’m not for a shallow one. A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.” He called on the new Democratic-controlled Congress to pass Medicare for All, codify a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, abolish ICE, and cut off funding to Israel, which he said was committing an ongoing genocide against Palestinians. All of this got huge cheers from the audience — some of whom, one presumes, also applauded Jeffries just one day earlier.

Depending on whom you ask, What’s Next was either a concerted effort to rally Democrats around an affordability agenda or moderates’ cynical attempt at co-opting voters’ populist rage. Across the street from the Mission Ballroom, a small group of protesters with Indivisible unfurled a giant banner that read “NO SCHUMER CORONATION.” Members of another group, posted up by one of the side stages hosting the “Do Issues Matter?” panel, told me they hoped the Democrats didn’t abandon their commitment to immigration reform and abortion rights. At the “AI safety breakfast,” one advocate of tech regulation told me there was little daylight between the organizations putting on the conference and its affiliated events — Majority Democrats, the Searchlight Institute, and the pro-AI regulation PAC Tomorrow Together — and the flailing Abundance movement. “They’re rebranding because no one likes abundance,” she said. “This is counter-programming to the populist left. They took a bunch of AI safety money to put on things like this.”

There were notable absences. Vermont senator and erstwhile presidential candidate Bernie Sanders was not in attendance, and neither was New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America recently urged to run for president. Slotkin may have name-checked El-Sayed, but he wasn’t there, either. Not even Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros – a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who won her race in a landslide and now represents the very district where the conference was held – was present. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a member of Majority Democrats who helped organize the event, told The Washington Post that he had personally invited Ocasio-Cortez.

Still, there were other representatives of the party’s left wing milling about, including Khanna, Van Hollen, and Angie Nixon, a DSA-backed Democrat who came within 3 percentage points of winning a Florida Senate seat. And regardless of their political leanings — and counter to the Democratic Party’s 2024 message that the economy was just fine, actually — nearly every single speaker decried the steadily increasing economic divide separating America’s billionaires from the shrinking middle class and the growing ranks of the working poor.

“We just won in a historic fashion, and I think everyone feels good about that,” said Morris Katz, a 26-year-old digital strategist whose roster of previous clients includes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. (Katz was also the driving force behind Senate contender Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after being accused of sexual assault.) “I think everyone is united under an anti-billionaire focus on affordability and corruption, and there’s a lot to feel good about.”
And what about the billionaire funding this very conference?

“If there are people who want to support where we’re headed, and the things we’re doing, great, everyone’s welcome,” Katz told me. The difference, he said, is whether Democrats let themselves be co-opted or corrupted by their donors. He pointed to outgoing Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott — who supercharged tech development in the state and whose campaign was largely funded by Elon Musk and data center developers — as an example of what could go wrong. “There’s a quid pro quo there that needs to be avoided at all costs. We need to be the anti-Big Tech party.”

Democrats are already heading in that direction. Khanna pointed out that one-third of the nation’s wealth is concentrated in the Silicon Valley district he represents. Jerusalem Demsas, founder of the liberal publication The Argument, urged legislators to rein in AI development. (“I know everyone here is in a good mood, and it’s about to not be a good mood,” she said before reminding the assembled legislators and political operatives that “what comes after winning is governing.”) At a press conference after her speech, Slotkin called for the establishment of a bipartisan, bicameral committee on AI akin to midcentury bodies created to regulate nuclear power. “While we’re bickering with each other — Democrats and Republicans — there’s an opportunity cost, and we have not done what we need to do on AI,” she said. “If we were healthy politically, we would have been working on this for five years straight.”

There was an obvious undercurrent of technopessimism throughout the weekend. News of the nationwide FAA ground stop broke minutes before a panel titled “How Weird Will AI Make 2028?” Though a faulty router was ultimately identified as the culprit, attendees — myself included — couldn’t help but speculate whether an AI cyberattack, or even just shoddy implementation of the FAA’s new AI tool, was actually to blame.

“It was clear that there is just a huge interest in AI here, and grappling with it, that sits across the party,” Rob Flaherty, the cofounder of the AI safety PAC Tomorrow Together told me. Flaherty’s organization hosted an off-the-record breakfast on AI safety. “We built it for 100 people, and 600 people showed up,” he said. The coffee ran out almost immediately, though there were somehow enough burritos to go around. Tomorrow Together’s polling, which was shared at the breakfast, indicates that voters don’t just hate data centers but have broadly soured on AI. They tie AI developments to broader economic concerns like rising utility bills and a worsening job market. Most importantly, voters don’t think the companies can be trusted to regulate themselves.
“Now it’s on Democrats to not just channel the anger and be the vessel for that anger but to actually enact the things that are going to alleviate the pain that people are feeling,” Flaherty told me.

But for Flaherty, who previously worked for Biden’s and Harris’ presidential campaigns, the conference “was less about a policy agenda and more about a theory of power” — one articulated by Bernie Sanders a decade ago. “If you look at the way people — James Talarico on down, Hakeem Jeffries on down — were speaking, it doesn’t sound dissimilar from the kinds of things Bernie was raising in 2016,” said Flaherty. “He rightly — and I was working on the other side — identified some of the economic discontent that a lot of people are feeling.”

Still, there’s a difference between Sanders’ vision of Medicare for All and, say, a public option — or what 2020 presidential hopeful Pete Buttigieg described as “Medicare for all who want it.” Both fall under the broad umbrella of universal healthcare, but the distinctions matter. Absent nitty-gritty policy discussions, however, it’s easy to get the sense that all voters — and all Democrats — want the same thing. Perhaps this is why, even among the professional Democrats in attendance, I met people who told me they wanted Democrats to prosecute ICE agents, enact a $25 an hour minimum wage, and pack the Supreme Court. At a certain point, I became desperate to find someone whose politics were a little more tepid.

My pleas were answered by Uriel Espinoza, a local Democrat whose friends introduced him as a centrist. Espinoza’s friends insisted that I join them for happy hour at a nearby brewery. (Espinoza said he rejects the centrist label, but broadly disagrees with the Democratic Socialists of America’s manifesto.) Their car wasn’t big enough to fit us all, but it didn’t matter. As four of us piled into the back seat of a Tesla whose driver — another member of the friend group — was blasting Drake, Espinoza told me he had once identified as a conservative. At the bar, he and another friend said the conference had been fun, if a little “East Coast consultant-y.”

Here was the mythical moderate voter in all his glory. He was even wearing a cowboy hat. And what did he want? Immigration reform, universal healthcare, and an economy that isn’t stacked against working people. There was a time, Espinoza told me, when he felt betrayed. “On certain things — like Israel, Gaza, Palestine, immigration — we are looking to our elected officials at the highest level, and we feel that they aren’t really delivering, or differentiating himself from Republicans,” he said.
I told him he sounded almost like a leftist.

“I’m also surprised, myself, because I’ve never thought of myself — and I don’t think of myself — as a socialist,” he told me. “I’m an entrepreneur. I’m pro-business, I’m pro-economy, but I’m also, at this point, pro-results.”
Update, November 17th: This piece has been updated to include Uriel Espinoza’s description of his political leanings.

items.title: Australia sanctions individuals and company involved in illegal West Bank settlements
paragraphs: Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank.
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”

Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers.

Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.

Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.

“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

items.title: Protest against talk by academic who made Arday plagiarism claim
paragraphs: Protesters appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into Oriel College
Hundreds of people have gathered to protest against a talk at an Oxford University college by the academic who accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism.
Stand Up To Racism organised a demonstration against Nathan Cofnas's talk at Oriel College, organised by Oxford Reform UK, on Tuesday evening.
Protesters, some with face masks on, appeared to try to block the entrance gates to stop people getting into the college before the talk.
Dozens of protesters held signs saying "Nathan Cofnas not welcome" and "Remember Professor Jason Arday".
Chants of "Nathan Cofnas shut him down" could be heard.
Cofnas, who has advocated for "race realism", wrote a blog accusing Prof Arday of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis.
Confas's talk was entitled "Is DEI (diversity, equality and inclusion) Undermining Higher Education?"
It prompted a weeks-long plagiarism row that saw 41-year-old Arday face intense public scrutiny about his work and other achievements.
Although he denied the allegations made against him, Arday resigned his post as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education. He was found dead at his home in south London on 14 August.
Theo Biggs, 20, who is a student at nearby Oxford Brookes University, said: "Oxford University is a prestigious university, and what is talked about here is talked about around the world.
"Giving this sort of conversation a platform is legitimising it essentially."

A course administrator at the university, who did not want to be named, said: "I've seen a lot of students of colour are feeling unwelcome, uncomfortable, frightened by the fact that Oriel and the wider university has not shut this down."

Another student added: "I've worked really hard to get here. I pay a lot of money to be here, and then me being a minority is like the biggest sin in the world. It's not something I want, it's not something I'm standing for at all."
Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor after the allegations of plagiarism that he denied
The talk's event page stated Cofnas "faced recent controversy after exposing the plagiarism of Jason Arday".

Cofnas has previously written that black people are less intelligent than other groups and would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment" under a meritocratic system.
He was suspended from Ghent University in Belgium in August before being reinstated after pressure by US ambassador Bill White.
On Thursday, protesters against the talk placed a Ku Klux Klan hood on a controversial statue of the 19th Century colonialist Cecil Rhodes at Oriel College.
In response to the protest, the college said it was "committed to upholding freedom of speech within the law and has a statutory duty to do so".
"We are also committed to promoting inclusion and maintaining an environment that is free from all forms of discrimination and harassment, including racial discrimination," it said.
It added that permitting the event "does not imply endorsement by the college of the views of its speakers".

items.title: Some EU countries ‘could accept unlimited young Britons’ under youth mobility scheme
paragraphs: EU countries including Germany could accept an unlimited number of young Britons under a youth mobility scheme, according to sources.

Fresh details on how a scheme might work have emerged with EU leaders and the UK expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each others territories from 2028.

The UK has insisted on a quota of EU citizens entering the UK under the scheme to guard against mass migration, but some countries have said they will not follow suit on the other side of the Channel and would be open to taking unlimited numbers.

The quota is expected to be worked out on a country-by-country basis with smaller countries such as Malta and Luxembourg seeking a system that will not be based on a per-capita quota per EU member state.
The youth mobility scheme for under-30s is expected to be sealed in principle as the EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday.

In what looks like a win for Andy Burnham, however, several diplomats have said the tricky question of EU students paying the same fees as their UK counterparts if studying at a UK university under the scheme would be postponed for six months.

This is to allow linkage with the Made in Europe legislation that will not reach its final stages until possibly April next year in a vote in the European parliament. The legislation is designed to give priority to EU supply chains in the car and other industries.
By linking the two issues the UK can get assurances that the final detail of the deal on mobility cannot be signed off unless it has been included in the Made in Europe legislation.

It is also understand that the majority of the 12-page draft joint statement has been agreed, with negotiations expected to continue to the wire and perhaps even during the summit between Burnham, the European Council leader, António Costa, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, which starts at 10am on Friday.

The details came as Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he came under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.
The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he also hopes to secure agreements on food and farming and emissions trading.

In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.

The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest.

While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked.

No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done.

These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be.

Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn.

In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all.

But after revealing his personal preference would be to fully rejoin the bloc, Burnham has encountered some resistance, including from within the cabinet, with some MPs with Leave-voting seats anxious about reopening the debate.

Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal.

In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.
“We’ll see how [Friday’s summit] goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.”
The prime minister denied that he was “jumping the gun” or “making any assumptions” about where the UK would end up – but pointed to polling which shows the public wants closer ties with the bloc.
Some Labour MPs, however, are concerned about the impact of freedom of movement in particular, as the debate around immigration in the UK has grown with the rise of Reform UK.
“I won’t get ahead of public opinion. I will listen to what the public feel is the right long term solution,” Burnham added.
While much of the deal expected to be agreed in Brussels on Friday is over the line, there are still tensions over the level of the cap on the youth mobility scheme cap, as well as over tuition fees.

Officials are also expected to discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €50bn (£40bn) safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

items.title: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
paragraphs: is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400. According to The Verge’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.

While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today. That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.

Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.

On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK.

items.title: California just banned Waymo from all state freeways
paragraphs: California has pulled the plug on Waymo’s driverless freeway rides across the entire state, citing potential safety hazards.

In a statement, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said that the ban went into effect on November 11th after two recent high-profile Bay Area incidents, in which Waymo robotaxis drove into an active construction closure on US-101 near Burlingame, and a separate run-in involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco.

In its statement, the DMV explicitly labeled Waymo’s freeway operations as an “imminent hazard to public safety,” noting that this isn’t an isolated glitch. Waymo has experienced “recurring incursions into active construction zones, the DMV said, arguing the company was putting road workers at risk.

Waymo has struggled with freeway operations over the years. The company has been testing its vehicles on California’s freeways since at least August 2024, before eventually opening up to public passengers in November 2025. Waymo voluntarily paused freeway operations in May 2026 over concerns about construction sites — but then resumed rides in late July.

Operating on freeways is crucial to Waymo’s robotaxi business; without freeways, the company will be forced to take longer routes on local roads that will force customers to pay more for their fares. On average, Waymo rides are already more expensive than human-driven Uber or Lyft trips.

In a statement, Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas said the company voluntarily paused freeway driving across all its markets to review performance, though its surface-street ride-hailing service remains unaffected. Waymo is currently collaborating with state regulators to safely resume highway operations.
“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Pappas said.

In order to get back on the freeway, Waymo will need to demonstrate it has taken sufficient action to improve its operation around construction zones, the DMV said. The company will need to submit evidence to the agency for review, at which point regulators will determine whether it can safely resume operations.

items.title: Church of England should protect 'every belief', King says
paragraphs: King Charles has said the Church of England does not just protect the Christian faith, but also the space "for every belief" within British society.
He was speaking in his role as Supreme Governor of the Church at the inauguration of a new term of its national assembly, General Synod.
While such comments have caused fierce theological debate in the past, they are consistent with the King's long-expressed beliefs.
Similar statements about the Church were also made by Queen Elizabeth II in a landmark speech given during her Diamond Jubilee.
The late Queen attended 10 Synod inauguration ceremonies since the assembly was established in 1970, though the then Earl of Wessex attended on her behalf at the last inauguration in 2021.

The day's ceremony started with a worship service at Westminster Abbey. The King and members of Synod then moved the short distance to Church House, the Church's administrative headquarters, for the Sovereign's address.

Speaking to the nearly 500 members of the assembly - including all the Church's bishops as well as clergy and lay people, many of whom were newly elected for a 5-year term - the King talked of his own deep faith and the way it guided him.
He then talked of a clear vision of the Church's public role.
"At a time when our society can feel divided, it is all the more important that the Church of England continues to extend its ministry among all the people of this country," the King said.

"The Church protects not just the Christian faith of all of us gathered in this room, but the very space for faith itself – of every belief – within our whole society and national discourse," he continued.

In an interview in 1994, the then Prince of Wales caused controversy by talking of a desire to be seen as "Defender of Faith" rather than "Defender of the Faith", the term by which sovereign leaders of the Church of England are referred.

He later clarified that his comments had been misinterpreted, saying he never intended to abandon his Church of England role, but could also act as a "protector of faiths" having long talked and written passionately about interfaith harmony and protecting everyone's right to worship.
In 2023 the King maintained his traditional coronation oaths, including a vow to be "Defender of the Faith", while also prominently incorporating multi-faith elements into the coronation ceremony.
But the King's comments today are reminiscent of a speech given by Queen Elizabeth II to an interfaith audience at Lambeth Palace in 2012.

She spoke of the role of the Church of England often being misunderstood, saying its duty was not to exclusively defend Anglicanism, or to exclude other religions, but to protect the free practice of all faiths in the UK.

Speaking today, the King did not speak directly of other contentious issues facing the Church such as safeguarding, or Christian nationalism, slavery reparations or the financial pressures on parishes
But it is clear that while this was something of a celebratory day for the Church, and particularly for the new members of Synod, there will be solemn and serious work to be done in the coming years.

items.title: JBL’s headphones that are great for in-flight entertainment are 67 percent off
paragraphs: writes about tech news, reviews gadgets, and helps readers save money by highlighting deals and product recommendations for The Verge.

If you’re looking to upgrade your headphones before the big wave of Black Friday deals arrives, you can buy JBL’s Tour One M3 for a new low price of $149 ($300 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from JBL. The deal is so good that my colleague John Higgins, The Verge’s audio and TV reviewer, popped in on his day off to tell us just how much of a steal they are at this price.

JBL’s Tour One M3 stand out largely because they come with the Smart Tx wireless audio transmitter. Frequent fliers will likely appreciate the accessory, which plugs into a plane’s in-flight entertainment system via a 3.5mm cable, allowing you to listen to audio wirelessly. It also works with other devices that lack Bluetooth support but have a headphone jack. The small touchscreen-equipped transmitter also lets you easily adjust the headphones’ noise cancellation, EQ settings, and volume. It can be used to answer calls, too.

Fancy tricks aside, the headphones get the essentials right. According to John, they offer excellent passive noise isolation, and their active noise cancellation is good enough to block out low-frequency sounds, like airplane engines. He also praises their overall sound quality, though he notes that JBL’s default tuning slightly affects midrange clarity, something you can easily fix by adjusting the EQ. They also support high-resolution lossless audio over the included USB-C or 3.5mm cable, plus spatial audio with head tracking. JBL says they can last up to 70 hours on a single charge with noise cancellation off — enough to get you through multiple long-haul flights — while the USB-C-chargeable transmitter offers up to 18 hours of battery life.

items.title: “We're not saying they're perfect” says architect fighting to save Melbourne's public housing blocks
paragraphs: Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of Melbourne’s public housing towers. In this interview, he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, Homes Victoria’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne’s public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials argue that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.
But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has prompted concern from the UN’s special rapporteur on housing, and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.
Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice Office.

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.
“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn’t do a refurbishment study on these estates,” Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.
“So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents.”

“We’re not saying that they’re in perfect condition,” he added. “We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these rapprochement studies need to occur.”
In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.
By avoiding the relocation of residents, Office estimates that a retrofit and infill approach would cost around $300 million less than demolition and rebuild.

“As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed,” said Robinson.
“We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market.”
The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR).
RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.
Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.
Formerly home to approximately 10,000 people, Flemington Estate’s four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria’s public housing stock.
Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.
Office has proposed retaining the estate’s 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill social housing units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.
Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.
Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.
“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.
As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.
Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be “community housing” – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.
Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.
Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.
“What they’re building is community housing, not public housing, so there’s no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.
“The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don’t want the public to know that it’s no longer public housing,” he continued.
“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we’re currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”

The issue is particularly charged in the context of Australia‘s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.
“Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right,” said Robinson.
“By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households.”

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council’s Legal and Social Issues Committee urging the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Valley Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.
This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we’ve presented to different ministers as well, and we’ve kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.
“It kind of suggests that perhaps they’re gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”
However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.
Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

A class action filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.
Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.
Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.
“We’ve gotten to a point where we feel we can’t just keep putting out these reports,” he said.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we’re now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what’s occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”
He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia’s prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.
“It’s really hard to find anyone who’s willing to talk about why they’re doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We’re alone.”
Dezeen put Robinson’s claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

items.title: Google’s Spark AI agent becomes ‘Tasks’ — and now it’s free
paragraphs: is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans, manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find recurring expenses you might not need.

Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or texting it.

Google first introduced its Spark AI agent in May, but it was only available to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The launch of tasks in Gemini brings Spark’s capabilities to all users in the US, Canada, Japan, Korea, Australia, and India. You can find tasks by opening Gemini and changing the toggle on the homepage from “Chat” to “Tasks.”

Tasks in Gemini is just one of the many agentic AI features that have emerged over the past year, including Claude Duet, OpenAI’s Dots, and Meta’s Muse. Google says Gemini will perform tasks in a “hardware-isolated virtual machine that’s dedicated to your account and never shared with other users.” You can also provide instructions for Gemini while it completes tasks. When performing more sensitive tasks, like purchasing an item, it will stop working and ask for your permission before following through.
