items.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
paragraphs: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.
Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.
He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.
But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."
The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.
There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.
But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".
McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".
The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.
He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.
In his wide-ranging 250 page report, external, Milburn proposes:
An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales
Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently
A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper
A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training
A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan
Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience
The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.
And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.

Milburn has said his plans are not about saving money - and his report says the government will not see overall savings from reduced benefit bills and higher tax receipts until 2036/27, when it will claw back £200m.
But by then, it assumes the share of 16–24-year-olds that are Neet will have gone down from 13% - one of the highest in Europe - to 5%, the lowest in the UK since records began.
Launching his report earlier on Tuesday, Milburn said "half measures will not do" because "the scale of the problem is just too big for that".
He added: "Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people, not because they lack talent, not because they lack ambition, not because they do not want to work.
"This is not a crisis of aspiration; it is a crisis of opportunity."
Milburn's report has no specific blueprint for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, where education, skills, health and local government are devolved.
He said the UK and devolved governments "should agree common definitions, a shared set of headline outcomes and a regular joint review of progress".
Scotland's Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said: "Where there is opportunity to collaborate with the UK government and others for the benefit of young people in Scotland, we will take it."
But she argued many of the reforms recommended for England, such as stronger vocational training, were already in place in Scotland.

A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "We stand ready to work with the UK government to ensure Wales benefits fully from any UK-wide measures that improve life chances through access to rewarding work."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he agreed "with the general drift of the Milburn report, but it's too little and too slow".
"We have a fundamental problem in Britain," he added. "Too many people are being encouraged to go on benefits, and training and apprenticeship schemes that take far too long."

Lib Dem treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said if the government wanted to get people into work, it should back high street firms "that give many their first job", scrap the "unfair jobs tax" and negotiate a new growth and defence partnership with the EU.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski described Milburn's proposals as a "flimsy sticking plaster" that intend to "slash support for disabled young people while subsidising corporations to hire cheap labour".

items.title: Iran launches a third round of strikes on Bahrain, host of U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet
paragraphs: A woman holds an Iranian flag as part of a pro-government campaign beneath a billboard depicting a launched missile, a man with a rifle, people and current and the late Revolutionary Guard missile force commanders with clenched fists, with a sign which reads in Farsi: "The sky is a place for our pride and loyalty," in downtown Tehran, Iran, Monday. Vahid Salemi/AP hide caption

CAIRO — Iran fired drones on Tuesday at a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain in the third Iranian attack in recent days on American military targets in the Persian Gulf island kingdom, and the U.S. retaliated by firing at Iranian targets along an important shipping route.

The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting, as Iran's targeting of Bahrain brought condemnations from the region. Analysts said stalled peace negotiations and Tehran's growing economic pressures were raising the risk of a substantial escalation.

Bahrain said that its air defense systems had successfully intercepted the "treacherous Iranian aerial attacks." The U.S. military likewise said the attack inflicted no damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel.
Hours later, a U.S. fighter jet carried out a strike on a missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a U.S. official said.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used in the strike on Qeshm Island and that the U.S. was responding to "aggression" toward U.S. personnel.
A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.

The U.S. military has periodically carried out what appear to be limited strikes on Qeshm Island and other Iranian targets this month. Iran's attack Tuesday was its third on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
This is a locator map for the Gulf Cooperation Council member states: Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and United Arab Emirates. AP hide caption

Iran has been suffering under a naval blockade that the U.S. has enforced on it for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for the world's energy supplies where Iran and its proxies have disrupted shipping since the war began Feb. 28.

U.S. President Donald Trump has been circumspect on his next steps for the Iran war, now in its eighth month despite an initial promise it would last only a matter of weeks. He has said new strikes are highly unlikely, but he has also sent a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East — and told Vice President JD Vance that talks aren't needed at this time.

Oil tankers moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection have helped return oil shipments from the Gulf to roughly prewar levels. The blockade, meanwhile, is damaging Iran's economy by curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.

Iran's attacks could signal a shift in its strategy after months during which it waited for an attack and then retaliated to target the operational capability of bases, Tehran-based security analyst Mostafa Najafi told The Associated Press.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, which has already sustained damage in previous attacks by Iran since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.

Iranian leaders will now be weighing whether "breaking the blockade through escalation is less costly than accepting its continuation," Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X.

"In other words, the risk of renewed war no longer depends solely on whether Trump decides to attack Iran again," he said. "It also depends on whether Tehran concludes that the costs of continued restraint have become greater than the risks of escalation."

With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group in the region, the combined U.S. naval assets in the Persian Gulf, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Mediterranean now exceed the force deployed when the U.S. and Israel launched the war.
The presence provides greater offensive firepower and missile interception capacity, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington aircraft carriers, as well as smaller U.S. Navy ships, which are in the region to maintain the blockade of Iranian shipping. U.S. Central Command wouldn't comment on whether it plans to keep all three carrier strike groups in the region.

Iran's attack on Bahrain on Tuesday came after it targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in the country on Friday, and on Sunday fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Despite claims of success, there appeared to be little or no damage done.
The attacks followed U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance operations, and Iran said it was retaliating.

"Continued aggression against the country's airspace, as well as the use of regional military bases and facilities for hostile acts against Iran, will not go unanswered," Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement.
Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned Iran's attack on Bahrain, calling it a violation of Bahrain's sovereignty and a threat to its security and stability.
Negotiations to end the war have stagnated, despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.

In a statement, Qatar said Iran's "continued attacks" on Bahrain "undermine diplomatic efforts" and Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari, speaking at a news briefing in Doha, warned that any escalation in fighting posed an "extremely grave danger" to the prospects of reaching an agreement.
The attacks are a sign that Tehran is growing impatient as its economic woes mount, said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defense analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

"Shooting at ships causes fear, but is not effective enough to change the strategic equation," Bruchmann told the AP. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week. This is not it — yet."
Iranian officials have termed the current situation "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it.
Tehran has said that it's open to a negotiated deal, but also signaled a readiness to escalate the conflict in the face of tightening sanctions and the blockade that are throttling Iran's economy.
Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's influential parliamentary chief, posted on social media on Monday that leaders view U.S. economic pressure as an effort to create a domestic "security crisis."

Iran has continued to attack ships seeking to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which leads from the Persian Gulf toward the open seas. In Yemen, Iran-backed Houthi rebels now have solidified their control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another critical shipping route.

items.title: Meta is testing a new standalone messaging app called Direct
paragraphs: Direct lets you access Instagram chats in a dedicated app, but it isn’t widely available yet.
Direct lets you access Instagram chats in a dedicated app, but it isn’t widely available yet.
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Meta announced Direct, a new messaging app from Instagram that it’s currently testing in Turkey and Thailand on iOS and Android. Direct is essentially Instagram’s direct messaging without Instagram’s other features. Meta says your Instagram chats will sync across both apps if you login with the same account. You can also sign up with an email or phone number, but Meta says if you use Direct without an Instagram account, “only your contacts can start a chat with you or add you to a group.”

This is far from Meta’s first messaging app — it also has Messenger, which requires a Facebook account to use, and WhatsApp, which Meta (then Facebook) acquired in 2014. Meta also recycled the “Direct” name, which it previously used for a Snapchat-like app it shut down several years ago.
The new Direct app has a UI similar to Instagram’s messaging tab, but with extra features for customizing chats and sending different types of media, including:
• Draw: Draw and sketch directly inside your chat threads.
• Notes: Catch quick updates from friends right at the top of your inbox.
• Stickers: Create custom stickers to express yourself and share with friends and family.
• Voice Effects: Add fun audio effects like crowd laughter or underwater sounds to your replies.
• Themes: Personalize your chat backgrounds with custom visual themes.
Meta says users have to be at least 13 years old to use Direct, and teens who log in with their Instagram account will have the same Teen Account messaging protections and restrictions on Direct.

items.title: Amflow’s new urban e-bike series is deliciously overpowered for flat city streets
paragraphs: DJI spinoff Amflow has spent the last couple of years shaking up the electric mountain bike (eMTB) market with ridiculously high-torque, lightweight models. Today, it’s bringing that same overengineered energy to pavement with the UE Series, its first urban commuter line.

The series consists of two models: the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro. Both pack 125Nm of torque, 1,100W of peak power, and an 8x max assist ratio capable of climbing 30 percent grades — all while operating quietly under 45dBA (quieter than a household refrigerator). A swappable 600Wh battery provides up to 132km (about 82 miles) of range and fast-charges from zero to 100 percent in 2 hours and 23 minutes.

While most city e-bikes deliver their power modestly, Amflow is strapping a mountain-bike-grade motor onto a 20.9 kg (46 pounds) upright step-through frame — and pricing it slightly below its flagship trail bikes. The UE Carbon starts at €3,099 (about $3,500 USD), while the Pro will sell for €3,499 ($3,900 USD).

But this isn’t just another commuter bike. With its proprietary Avinox drivetrain, Amflow has been ahead of the curve in blending consumer gadget UX — features like wireless phone charging, Apple Watch proximity unlock, Find My integration, and camera controls — with serious hardware specs. That’s one of the reasons why The Verge’s own Thomas Ricker has been so bullish on the brand for the past few years.

With 125Nm of max torque and 1,100W of peak power, the Avinox M2 in the UE Series is slightly more dialed back from Amflow’s 150Nm flagship eMTBs. That said, 125Nm is still massive overkill for flat city streets — but it won’t hurt to have it when encountering any grades over 30 percent. A new Auto Boost mode automatically dumps extra power when starting at a traffic light or hitting a steep hill. And traction control will help prevent any spin-outs on wet asphalt.

The 600Wh removable battery is good for up 82 miles in Eco mode — and likely less than that while relying on higher levels of assist. It’s worth noting that the 1,100W peak power and 8x assist ratios will likely be software-capped depending on where you live and what regulations allow.

As a brand within the larger DJI ecosystem, Amflow loves to integrate a lot of tech into its bikes. A 1.4 inch touchscreen is integrated into the handlebars alongside a 15W wireless phone charger — plus a 20W USB-C charger, if you prefer. The cockpit also features plenty of Apple tie-ins, like the aforementioned Find My tracker and Apple Watch proximity unlocking. The UE can also pair with a heart rate monitor, allowing riders to set a target heart rate zone that will dictate how much pedal assist the bike provides. And, of course, there’s direct recording controls for DJI Osmo cameras, in case you like to film your rides.

Additional security is provided by a built-in 10mm hardened steel wheel lock keyed to match the removable battery. And if the bike is paired with “Lost Mode” in the Amflow app, the user can remotely brick the drive system if the bike ever gets stolen.
There’s plenty of commuter-friendly touches, like a 65mm suspension fork, suspension dropper seatpost, and heavy-duty racks rated for 20kg (44 pounds) on the front and 27kg (60 pounds) on the rear.
The bikes are on sale globally starting today via Amflow’s website and retail partners. The company says a smaller XS frame size is coming in 2027 for shorter riders.

items.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him
paragraphs: Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation.
"I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia.
But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company.
The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely.
The company's board is investigating his conduct, which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive.
The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang.

Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead.
The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life".
Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal.
Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics".

"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added.

Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company.
Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return.
Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement.
On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course.

While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law."

items.title: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
paragraphs: The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."

items.title: Who to watch in Spain's election race
paragraphs: Sánchez has led the Socialists for the past 12 years, and Spain since 2018.
He has built a reputation as a political survivor but this election - his sixth in 11 years - could be his toughest yet.
Sánchez called the snap election eight months early, seeking to focus on resolving Spain's housing crisis, and vowing "an epic comeback of a progressive Spain" at the ballot box.

But he and his party have been embroiled in a series of corruption scandals, a migrant crisis in Spain's Ceuta exclave on the Moroccan border and two deadly rail disasters nine months apart. The most recent tragedy claimed 69 lives at Urda on 28 October and overshadowed the start of the campaign.
The Socialist leader has been written off in politics before, only to stage comebacks, notably in 2017 and 2023.
He can point to a projected 2.6% annual growth in the Spanish economy in 2026, fuelled by tourism, but the graft cases against his inner circle and family are not going away.

José Luis Ábalos, who was transport minister in Sánchez's government, is now serving a 24-year prison sentence for accepting kickbacks, meanwhile leading party figure Santos Cerdán awaits trial for alleged bribery and denies wrongdoing.

Sánchez's wife, Begoña Gómez, faces trial over allegations of influence peddling and embezzlement while his brother, David Sánchez, has been banned from public office for nine years for misconduct. Both deny doing anything wrong.
In a defiant message, Begoña Gómez made her first party speech at the Socialist campaign launch, calling for the backing of Spanish women, "because when women step forward, all of Spain follows".
Sánchez's fate could be sealed by the rise of Abascal's anti-immigration, populist Vox - with opinion polls putting them in a comfortable third place and taking votes from the Socialists.

Abascal, 50, denies his party is far-right and has succeeded in bringing Vox into the mainstream, attracting record ratings on one of Spanish state TV's primetime entertainment shows during the campaign.

Repatriating migrants "in an illegal situation" and "remigration" of foreigners who do not contribute to Spain are big themes for Abascal, who has accused Pedro Sánchez of promoting an "act of invasion" with his policies.
He has promised to use the Spanish navy to defend the national borders and "send a message to the world that there is no room here for all of Africa and all of the Americas".
The Vox leader joined the PP aged 18, becoming a local councillor first and then an MP in the Basque regional parliament.

His political trajectory was closely shaped by his family's experience of threats and intimidation by Basque militant group Eta. Both his father and grandfather, who held public office, were targeted because of their political roles.

He left the conservatives in 2013, founding Vox the following year and becoming a Spanish MP in 2019, when Vox became the first hard-right party in decades to establish a significant presence in Congress.
Vox has adopted the Trump-inspired slogan "Make Spain Great Again" and advocates a strongly centralised vision of the country strongly opposed to the independence movement in Catalonia.
Critics have described the party's ideology as reminiscent of aspects of the era of dictator Francisco Franco era, which Vox rejects.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, 48, has been president of the Madrid region since 2019 and has become one of the most influential figures within the People's Party. She leads one of the PP's strongest electoral bastions, with conservatives having ruled the region for the past 31 years.

Ayuso has built a distinct political profile that often sets her apart from the party establishment. Her direct communication style and informal use of language have helped her connect with voters and attract significant media attention.
Her tenure has not been without controversy. Her partner has been the subject of a judicial investigation relating to alleged tax offences and document forgery, allegations he denies.

Opposition parties have also questioned the Madrid regional government's purchase of a luxury penthouse for official use. Critics have challenged the rationale behind the acquisition, while regional authorities have maintained that it was intended as a government workspace.

Socialist Carlos Cuerpo, 46, was chosen by Pedro Sánchez to take charge as interim transport minister after the Urda rail disaster and has become key to his election team. Cuerpo climbed the ranks through the economy ministry and became minister of economy, trade and business in 2023.

He has been ranked as best-regarded politician among the Spanish public, according to the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), and, when asked about his political ambitions has called himself "a team player, and I am committed to the team".
In the same light, Sánchez has said: "I believe politics is a team sport; on the opposing team we have Feijóo and Abascal, and on my team we have Carlos Cuerpo."

Catalonia's Socialist president Salvador Illa is also one to watch. He served as Spain's health minister during the Covid pandemic and some have viewed him as a potential successor as Socialist leader, even though he has backed Sánchez to remain as leader.

items.title: Perron shapes Quebec kitchen around tea collection
paragraphs: A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house’s renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.
Perron overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.
Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.
The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.
“For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements,” said Perron founder Nathalie Perron.
“We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her.”
The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.
At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her “teahouse”.
Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.
“Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life,” said Perron.
An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.
The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.
Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.
Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.
Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.
Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.
Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.
Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.
A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand JETA adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.
“It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to,” said the studio.
Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron’s home.

items.title: Jensen Huang to testify before Congress on ‘potential breach of national security’
paragraphs: Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”

The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.

Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.

A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce, under its secretary, Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by the attorney general, Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.

In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.

items.title: Hunger Games prequel splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
paragraphs: Joseph Zada plays Haymitch Abernathy at the age of 16

Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."
Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
Kieran Culkin plays Hunger Games host Caesar Flickerman
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire, external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times, external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter, external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."
And Time Out's four-star review, external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

items.title: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
paragraphs: President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.

In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."
CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.
Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.
Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.
The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.
During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.
"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."

In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.
He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator in indirect talks with the US, was similarly dismissive of the CNN report.
"Same false flags, same war mongering, new logos," he posted on X.
Mick Mulroy, a former CIA paramilitary officer and deputy assistant defence secretary, told the BBC: "A dirty bomb is not difficult to make or deploy."
"Although it is not a weapon of mass destruction, it can be a weapon of mass disruption," he added.

Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.
"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."
It comes as intelligence officials and members of the Trump administration seek congressional renewal of a key national security law.
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), which allows the US to ​spy on foreign nationals, expires next March.

items.title: Huang says he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia as he agrees to testify to Congress
paragraphs: A pedestrian walks in front of a Nvidia sign outside the company's headquarters on Nov. 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif. after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images hide caption

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board of directors allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," wrote Huang in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."

"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.

Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.
Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
Later Tuesday, investors will hear directly for the first time from Nvidia's new acting CEO, Colette Kress, when the company announces its quarterly earnings after markets close for the day.

items.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO
paragraphs: Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company on Thursday.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.

Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close on Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.
The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and employees who reported to him.

Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications .
Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues.

The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions.
Huang’s full statement is published below.

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

items.title: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule
paragraphs: At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.

“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.

Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.

Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.

As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.

Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.

Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.

A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.

Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.

One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.

They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”

In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.

Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.

“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.

The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

items.title: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
paragraphs: The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.

The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local ⁠time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital ​San José, the Red Cross ‌reported.
President Laura Fernández condemned ‌the attack in a video message.

“I am filled with indignation and outrage over ‌the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodríguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernández said.

The attorney general, Carlo Díaz, told the local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract ‌killing, probably linked to the allegations Rodríguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he ​was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Díaz said, adding that Rodríguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a ⁠signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Díaz pledged efforts to ​hold those responsible ​for the murder accountable.

The last such ​attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when the radio ​producer Parmenio ‌Medina was gunned ​down on a ​Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodríguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

items.title: ‘Spared a lot’: Kessler twins explained assisted dying decision in final letter
paragraphs: Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together.
The German sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living.
In a letter released by a friend, the 89-year-olds wrote: “Dear friends, we’re sorry that we’ve chosen to go this way, but due to our medical conditions we had no quality of life any more.
“Apart from our heart problems, we no longer have our senses of taste and smell. On top of that Ellen has suffered a brain stem stroke, and as a result we’ve reached rock bottom.”

Because they had “entered the world together”, they wished “to depart it together the same way”, they added, concluding: “Don’t be sad; we’re happy that assisted dying exists, because certainly as a result we will have been spared a lot.”
They signed off: “Wishing you all the very best. We’ll see you on Cloud 9.”

The sisters died on 18 November last year , assisted by a doctor and a lawyer, in the villa they shared in the Grünwald district of Munich in Germany, which was divided into two mirrored halves, one for each.
They had planned the process together, working with an assisted dying organisation, but had kept this from their friends.

The letters were posted into the letter boxes of people close to them on the evening before their deaths, with a handwritten instruction on the envelope: “Don’t open until 17 November.” Inside each envelope they had placed the gift of a piece of their jewellery.

Bibi Johns, a 97-year-old actor and the singers’ closest friend, the three having met on the set of the 1959 film La Paloma, said she heard of their deaths on the radio before she had had the chance to open the letter from them.
“It was a shock,” she told the newspaper Bild. “Alice and Ellen were like sisters to me. For me it feels as if they have merely gone on a long journey. I’m still waiting for them to call me up.”
They bequeathed to her a gold pendant depicting the heads of two signs of the zodiac, a gift in 1968 from the French singer Marcel Amont to his then-partner Alice.

The year before their deaths, in an interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera, the sisters said their wish was “to leave together, on the same day … the idea that one of the two will go first is very difficult to bear”. In their lifetimes they had also made a pact that neither would marry.

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

items.title: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
paragraphs: Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.

The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.

The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.

Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.

That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.

Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.

It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.

Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.

Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.

Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.

If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.

Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.

A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.

The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.

Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.
