items.title: Henry Nowak killer applies to appeal against conviction
paragraphs: Vickrum Digwa, who fatally stabbed 18-year-old Henry Nowak in Southampton in 2025, is also seeking a sentence review
The man jailed for murdering Henry Nowak has applied to appeal against his conviction.

Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed the 18-year-old student with a large dagger in Belmont Road, Southampton, on 3 December 2025, has also asked the Supreme Court to review his sentence, his lawyers have confirmed.
Earlier this month the Court of Appeal raised his minimum term from 21 to 25 years, after the Attorney General argued it was unduly lenient.
The BBC understands Digwa wants to argue that his conviction for murder is unsafe on four grounds. The applications do not mean Digwa will automatically get any further hearings or reviews.
Imran Khan and Partners, Digwa's lawyers, said: "An application has been lodged seeking to appeal against Vickrum Singh Digwa's conviction.
"That application concerns the safety of the conviction and is separate from the proceedings concerning sentence."
Henry Nowak, 18, was stabbed to death in Southampton in December 2025
Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was stabbed to death with a 21cm (8in) kirpan, a religious blade that Digwa said he carried as part of his Sikh faith.

Digwa, then 22, told police that Nowak had attacked and racially abused him, which led to Nowak being handcuffed as he lay dying. The trial judge later found Digwa's claims of racism to be a lie and there was no evidence Nowak was racist.
Digwa was jailed for life at Southampton Crown Court in June with a minimum term of 21 years.

One of the four grounds on which Digwa plans to challenge his murder conviction is that the trial judge wrongly excluded from evidence WhatsApp messages Nowak sent when he was about 13, which Digwa suggested displayed a history of racist language.
The messages were found by police during their review of Nowak's phone but the judge ruled them irrelevant and inadmissible.
Digwa is also seeking to appeal his conviction on the basis the jury should not have been told that police had secretly recorded him confessing to the stabbing.
The recording, he argues, breaks evidence rules relating to such material.
Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr increased Digwa's minimum term to 25 years

On 5 November, the Court of Appeal ruled that the trial judge had been right to calculate Digwa's minimum term from a starting point of 15 years as there had been no evidence he had planned to use the knife as a weapon.
Had that been the case, the starting point under sentencing law for murder would have been 25 years.

But the Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr said the final figure of 21 years had been too low because it understated Digwa's repeated use of the knife and the "deliberate cruelty, additional suffering and obstruction" that followed.
She and two other senior judges ordered "a very significant uplift ... to reflect the use of the large kirpan alone" and extended the minimum term to 25 years.
Digwa and his lawyers are seeking a review of how the judges reached that figure.

"The Court of Appeal upheld the sentencing judge's finding that Vickrum Singh Digwa had not taken the kirpan to the scene intending to commit an offence or intending to have it available for use as a weapon," his lawyers said in a statement.
"The court nevertheless concluded that the circumstances surrounding the weapon justified a very significant uplift and ultimately substituted a 25-year minimum term.
"The application therefore raises an issue of wider importance."
The Supreme Court reviews relatively few criminal cases and only does so where a point of law is disputed and it has wider implications for other cases.

items.title: We can't afford to hire under-25s, say firms. Will Milburn plans help?
paragraphs: ByNick Edser and Simon BrowningBusiness reporters

Lowering employers' National Insurance (NI) payments for those between 21 and 24, and cash incentives to take on some workers are among proposals put forward in Alan Milburn's report to get more 18-24 year-olds working.
Many companies have complained that recent increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to take on staff.
We talked to firms and business groups about the issues they face when hiring younger works and what they make of the proposals.
Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says he cannot justify the extra cost of training up new staff
Cutting NI costs is "right in the sweet spot of what firms need to hit the hire button", said the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC).
The Milburn report proposes NI thresholds could be raised over the next five years, from £5,000 to £10,000 for those aged 21 to 24, and suggests prioritising the retail and hospitality sectors.
Bournemouth-based café owner Ben Blades says the high costs he faces currently make it difficult to employ young people with no work experience.
"My labour costs are already over 45%. We simply cannot justify the extra cost to put on an extra staff member to train someone up for three months," he says.
"In hospitality our margins have been squeezed and squeezed and squeezed"
As a result, he says it currently makes more sense to employ someone who already has experience.
Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, says the recommendation to raise the threshold is "the right one" and "would be an immediate shot in the arm for job creation".
But the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) argues the Milburn report does not go far enough in tackling costs facing businesses.
It says while the NI proposal is welcome, the change should be wider than just retail and hospitality, otherwise it "risks adding complexity and blocking off potential career paths".
Ally Fir says if a state scheme was running she'd "jump on it right away"
Other proposals put forward by the Milburn review include cash incentives to employ younger workers.

Employers who take on any young person who has been Neet - not in education, employment or training - for six months should receive a £3,000 payment, and small businesses - with less than 50 employees - that do so should receive an extra £2,000
There would also be an extra £2,000 payment if the young person has been in care or is disabled.
Ally Fir runs a bookshop in Westbourne, alongside her partner Matt, and thinks more state support is needed.
She says incentivised schemes for small business "would help us to employ more, especially young people. If a scheme like that was going we'd jump on it right away."
Fir says she gets job applications "every single day". She'd like to take more people on but "it is the cost of employing people that makes that impossible".
Tom Parsons has already had experience of using government schemes to employ young people at his design consultancy, Aetha, in Poole, Dorset.
The Kickstart Scheme in 2020 meant he could take on two young people in fully funded six-month job placements offering 25 hours a week.
Tom Parsons says the old Kickstart Scheme was a game-changer for those employed under it

"One of them stayed with us for five years and the other one I think about three years. And it completely changed the game for them," Tom told the BBC. "So if there was a scheme like that, again, that would really help us."
He says he wants to employ young people but costs remain a huge barrier.
One of the government's flagship employment rights reforms risks weakening the hiring of young people, according to Milburn's report.
Ministers are abolishing what they call ''exploitative'' zero-hours contracts and replacing them with guaranteed hours contracts which would be based on the number of hours people normally work.
Much of the detail is yet to be finalised but the Employment Rights Act is due to be enacted next year.
Milburn is concerned that the changes could cause problems "at a time when the youth labour market is already weak'.'
The REC said companies were "particularly worried" over the guaranteed hours measure.
It added that addressing the Neets problem gave ministers "the perfect opportunity" to reconsider the issue.
Young people should have a legal right to a route into education, training or work, and would be supported to do so under an "opportunity guarantee", Milburn has proposed.
This could help firms which are struggling to recruit. Thirty-five-year-old Dean Greene, a sales director at waste management facility Williams Environmental, says it's tricky finding staff.
"We didn't get many applicants for it at all," says Greene, referencing an ad for a marketing and sales role.
"There wasn't a huge uptake from that sort of 16-to-24 range," he adds.
He thinks the lack of applicants may be because the waste industry is perceived as "mucky and dirty", but he is confident many would be interested if they knew the job was available.
Pointing to himself as an example of progressing in the industry, he tells me how he started as an admin officer scanning paperwork at 18 before remaining with the company for 17 years.
Share your experiences and ask your questions.

items.title: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack
paragraphs: The BBC's Sarah Rainsford spoke to residents near the site of the overnight strike.

items.title: How the attack on Putin's prized Crimean Bridge unfolded
paragraphs: The attack on the strategic Crimean Bridge was carried out gradually to cut across several layers of defence, Kyiv confirmed on Tuesday.

For several weeks Ukraine's Security Service and its General Staff gradually destroyed air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets, and other designated targets, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

A significant strike had already been reported on 16 November, when drones hit the bridge at night. Traffic was paused briefly then reinstated, and although the arch over the road section was visibly damaged, the structure remained standing.
But that hit turned out to have been only the penultimate stage of a complex attack.
In the early hours of 17 November, the final strikes dealt a fatal blow to the weakened arch structure.

One verified video - filmed from a camera on board a Ukrainian-made Flamingo missile - shows the weapon approaching the main span of the bridge and heading towards the steel arches, with the footage freezing just before impact.

The Flamingo had potentially been modified to be controlled remotely, which improved its accuracy enough to strike the bridge supports, munitions expert Justin Bronk, from the Royal United Services Institute said.
The missile's "very heavy warhead" made it "more suitable" for attacking the bridge's reinforced concrete spans and supports, Bronk added.

Zelensky later confirmed that several types of missiles and drones had been employed in the attack, which led the massive road arch - weighing thousands of tonnes and measuring about 227m in length - to collapse into the strait.
Daylight images taken from the shores of Crimea to the north show a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was too dragged below into the sea.

This is clearly critical damage to the crossing. Far from just being a decorative feature of the bridge, the arch played a structural role, transferring loads and supporting the span and helping to ensure the stability of the entire structure.

The parallel arch supporting the railway section has remained standing, although it may also have been damaged. All traffic on the bridge was initially suspended, though trains were later allowed to resume running.

But the damage to the bridge's main span is "catastrophic", Colin Capriani, a structural engineer from Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told BBC Verify. It was "very hard to envisage" how the bridge could be rebuilt given it is clearly well within range of Ukrainian weaponry, Capriani added.
Major attacks in 2022 and 2023 had already caused serious damage to the road spans of the bridge, but the structure survived.

The difference this time is "the most critical and vulnerable part of the bridge has been hit", said David MacKenzie of engineering consultancy COWI, adding that "although the wreckage of the bridge can be cleared fairly quickly, reinstating full road traffic will take over a year".

Moscow uses Crimea as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it also carries out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.

The attack comes after a summer of frequent strikes on Crimea, dictated by Ukraine's stated goal of cutting the peninsula off from Russia. At the time, Kyiv vowed to turn the Crimean Peninsula "into an island".
Now - although it is too early to speak of a complete blockade of Crimea – the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis has increased significantly.

There is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. However, Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar, which has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

Moscow can also still utilise the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited - and anything on the Black Sea has become vulnerable to attack. Resupplying Crimea by sea is risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge - particularly its enormous arch - may have blocked the shipping channel. This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including the occupied cities of Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Away from the operational value of the damage to the bridge, the symbolic significance remains.
In 2018, Putin triumphantly drove over the bridge representing the unification of Russia and Crimea in a Russian-made truck. That section of the road now lies on the seabed.

Nearly five years since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin continues to wreak destruction on Ukraine's civilian population, but his most prized symbols of power are increasingly threatened by Kyiv's reach.

items.title: SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration
paragraphs: Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.
The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.
Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.
“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.
This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.
Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.
SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.
It is part of a wider renovation SOM announced for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.
SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.
“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.
“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”
SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO becomes a political proxy war
paragraphs: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers.

The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender.

We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era.

The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls.

Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients.
Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned. Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions.

The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China, given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them.
Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose.
Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left.

Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him.

The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang.
Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder.

“This week is seeing a long overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán, a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI.

Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “key man risk”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible.

“Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said.

Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are not likely successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis.

Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue.
‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang
Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule

A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken.

Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage.

The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. Transportation secretary Sean Duffy attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”.

Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.”

Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed. On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure. On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced.

These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities?

I don’t know what’s causing so much mayhem. The absence of a unified explanation in the face of so many similar incidents remains maddening. We’ll have to sit with the uncertainty until answers arrive.
In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.”
California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking
Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
Italy fines Meta $887m for accessing Android users’ photos and videos

items.title: Out of work and not in college: How quickly could Milburn's plans help you?
paragraphs: Alan Milburn has said the country needs a "complete system reset" to bring down the number of young people not in work or education - known as "Neets".

In a major review, published on Tuesday,, external he suggested a raft of proposals to address the problem, which mostly cover England but he says can be adapted in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.

Each of his recommendations will need to be accepted by the government and implemented and paid for before they become reality - and that could take some time. So how might today's proposals affect you if you are Neet?
At the heart of the recommendations, Milburn says, is a new Youth Opportunity Service. He wants this to be implemented locally, with each area drawing up a plan to help their own young people.
It would bring together employment, careers, health and practical support, with each young person getting a named adviser and a personalised plan.
Milburn wants areas to begin building their Youth Opportunity Service from 2027, with one in place everywhere by the end of 2029.

Within 14 days of entering the service, a young person would then meet with a named adviser. Within four weeks, they would have their "personalised participation plan", setting out what both the support services and the young person involved would do, and when.
Jobs wise, Milburn wants there to be initiatives like work placements of up to 12 weeks, structured volunteering opportunities, and help to create businesses.
He also wants those who remain Neet - despite enagaging with support - to be provided with a paid six-month job, funded by the government.
The government has already committed to a legal guarantee of job support in theory, but the exact workings still need to be worked out.
Alongside more work opportunities, Milburn wants a "major expansion" in further education for 18- to 24 year-olds, as well as more apprenticeship places.
Over the next decade, he wants the number of young people completing an apprenticeship to double, and for apprenticeships to rival university as an option for school leavers.
Colleges should also get new funding for participation and work-readiness, the review says, initially targeted at 16- and 17-year-olds who are Neet or at serious risk of becoming so.
He also wants the government to develop new industry-led technical colleges and specialist campuses.
If the reforms are enacted, Milburn says young people should have better access to high-quality further education and apprenticeships by 2028.
Under the proposals, schools, colleges and universities would be judged by whether pupils make successful transitions into further learning and work, rather than just academic achievements.
By 2036, he wants 35% of each year group to have started a high-quality apprenticeship by age 25.
Milburn has said he wants a fundamental transformation of how mental health support for young people is delivered.
Young people who are Neet should be guaranteed fast-track access to services within three months, according to his recommendations.

This would include things like vocational rehabilitation, talking therapies and counselling as part of a young person's plan with their local Youth Opportunity Service - which would be rolled out between 2027 and 2029 under the plans.
There has been a big rise in mental distress among children and young people in recent years, and Milburn's report comes at a time the NHS is facing huge pressures.
Milburn wants mental health support to be available for all young people digitally, without needing a diagnosis.
Some areas are already using these approaches, but scaling them up would be a major challenge and would take a long time to introduce across the board.

Plus, Milburn wants "fitness to work" notes to be taken out of the hands of GPs and put into community work and health teams, and for them to be "a trigger for help - not simply a certificate of absence".
Milburn wants these changes to begin in 2027 and would be linked to the Youth Opportunity Service rollout, which would be complete by 2029 under the plans.

Milburn has said he wants companies to be incentivised to employ more young people, with the report highlighting a competitive jobs market and applicants who often fail to hear back from potential employers.
The report includes three asks of employers: to create more genuine first jobs, more first-job apprenticeships and much wider access to meaningful work experience.
Plus, Milburn wants large employers to find ways of responding to rejected job applicants.
These changes should be felt by both employers and the young people looking for jobs by 2029, the report says.
To achieve this, the report suggests a £3,000 payment for employers who take on someone who has been Neet for six months, with a further premium of £2,000 available if they are a small business.
An extra payment of £2,000 would go to employers taking on somebody taking substantially greater barriers, such as care leavers or disabled young people.
These payments are proposed to be part of changes to the Youth Jobs Grant - which already exists, external - but they would expand under Milburn's proposals from 2027.
Share your experiences and ask your questions.

items.title: Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
paragraphs: Warning: This article contains references to suicide
Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".
The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.
But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.
"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.
"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."
The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".
"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.
"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.
"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.
"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.
But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.
"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.
"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.
"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.
"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.
"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.
"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."
If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

items.title: I tried the Funbox kids' 3D printer with my daughter – but would I recommend it?
paragraphs: A truly kids-focused 3D printer, which is accessible and simple to use. It's built fairly well, but comes with some key compromises in regard to size and build complexity. It's a fun toy, and a good introduction to 3D printing for younger children.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

I was captivated by the idea of a 3D printer designed for children, so I jumped at the chance to let my nine-year-old try the Funbox. She’s wanted a 3D printer for ages. I’ve held out, partly because of the cost and partly because of the inevitable tide of tiny plastic things that would end up around the house.

The Funbox is a compact, good-looking printer made by Ugee. It's fully enclosed for safety, has a clean air filter, is anti-scald and you can create with just a tap via the app. With Christmas coming up, plenty of parents will be hunting for the right option for their kids, so I want to be honest about whether this is it. Does this compare to the best 3D printers?

The external design is delightful. Ugee has nailed the look for kids: it’s cute, it has minimal buttons and fuss, and mine arrived in baby blue. A pack of stickers in the box lets your child decorate it themselves.

The inside is just as accessible. The build plate is easy to put in place and everything is clearly marked to show you how to get started (although we did make a wrong turn by not actually putting the plate in the first time around as you can see above – oops!).

Loading filament is simple, though it can be a bit fiddly for small fingers. It is pretty much plug and play – setup took me about 20 minutes, and my daughter was able to manage the first print pretty much independently with minimal interference, only some instruction. Bear in mind, the build space is small, so this printer is best for smaller prints. You can keep an eye on your print via the camera, which links to the app – my daughter was fascinated by this part.

Designs come from a marketplace in the Funbox app, available for mobile or tablet. It should be simple to use, but it’s glitchy. On our Huion tablet, the ‘start’ button was hidden behind the notch and there was no way to scroll or move the screen to reach it. That forced us onto the mobile app, which wasn’t ideal when I wanted my daughter to use the printer independently, without borrowing my phone.
For the most part, the Funbox worked as expected. My daughter could pick a print and start it herself, and she really enjoyed the process.

The small build volume is the main constraint. Many designs have to be printed in parts and assembled, which is fine if you stick to small prints. For anything more complex, you’ll need to be ready to help with sticking or putting pieces together. It also prints in a single colour at a time.

Most of the toys we printed turned out well, especially single-piece prints with no moving parts. The detail was good, and the results matched what the marketplace listings promised. Highlights include a cat hair comb, a skull and crossbones hair slide and a phone holder, which would hold my phone if it was the right size (note: must check next time).

Functional toys were a different story. We made a couple of fidget toys that couldn’t do their job without breaking. That could be down to the third-party design, or to the filament being too brittle for the purpose. We couldn’t tell which.
That fits what this printer is: a starter machine built for fun, not one that delivers polished, fully functional prints every time.
We haven’t yet tested the AI 3D model builder, which turns your child’s drawing into a printable 3D model. We’ll cover our experience of it in a separate piece.
The Funbox costs $299/£318 but is often on sale for $279/£289. Whether that’s reasonable depends on who you're buying it for.

For my nine-year-old, I’d rather take on the steeper learning curve of a basic ‘grown-up’ printer like the Bambu Lab A1, which I’d expect to give better-quality prints for similar money. It’s less approachable for a child to use alone, but the results would be worth it for her. For a younger child, though, the Funbox’s ease of use and friendly design make a stronger case, and I think they justify the price.
If you want a genuinely child-focused printer, this is a good option. Just be aware you’re trading away print size and complexity.
Choose your designs carefully. Ugee’s own are reliable, but third-party designs from the marketplace are hit and miss.
If your child is at the upper end of the age range (nine to 12), consider a basic printer from one of the adult-focused brands instead. For younger children, the Funbox is the easier fit.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 1
paragraphs: Nvidia is a big tech company. Its boss, Jensen Huang, leaves his job suddenly. The company’s stock price falls.

Huang leaves after news about his relationship with a woman who may be a spy for China. Nvidia chooses another boss for some time. So the business stays safe. Experts say that it will be very hard to find a new leader. Huang is the boss for 33 years.
Now, US officials want to check if Nvidia breaks any rules. The company sells computer parts to China. This big problem may make trade between the US and China more difficult.

Difficult words: suddenly (quickly, without a plan), stock price (how much one part of a company costs), spy (a person who gets information about other people or countries and they do not know about it).

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 2
paragraphs: Nvidia’s share price dropped quickly after its CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned.
He left the company after facing serious investigations over a personal affair with a woman who was a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a second affair with a company manager.

To keep business running smoothly, Nvidia named its finance boss as temporary leader. Experts say replacing Huang will be very difficult because he led the company for 33 years and was very important to its success in AI.

US officials plan to investigate what the company knew about the spying and whether Nvidia broke rules by selling computer chips to China. This problem could lead to stricter US trade laws and increased tension between America and China.

Difficult words: spy (a person secretly collecting and reporting sensitive information for a foreign government or competitor), temporary (when something lasts for only some time), tension (a state of difficult relations between countries or people).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends – level 3
paragraphs: Nvidia’s share price dropped sharply after its co-founder and longtime boss, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned. His decision followed growing pressure and a company investigation into his secret relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China.

Media reports also revealed a second affair with an executive inside Nvidia. To keep the business stable during this difficult change, the company appointed its finance chief as interim CEO to reassure investors and maintain stability during the unexpected leadership change. However, business experts warn that replacing Huang will be very hard, because he led Nvidia for 33 years and had no clear plan for a successor.

Beyond problems inside the company, the scandal raises serious questions about whether Nvidia broke US rules by selling advanced computer chips to China. Experts expect US politicians and police to investigate the company closely. They warn that Nvidia’s weaker influence in Washington could lead to stricter trade limits and increase political tension between the US and China.

Difficult words: executive (a person with senior managerial responsibility in a business organization), interim (temporary), successor (a person who takes over a job, office, or position after someone else leaves).

items.title: Paul Kelly pleads for Albanese to ‘show some backbone’ over AI as creatives campaign for copyright protections
paragraphs: Australia’s creative community has launched a major campaign pleading with the Albanese government not to water down copyright law amid furious lobbying from AI companies, ahead of Wednesday night’s Aria awards.

Music legends Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly and Peter Garrett are among those backing the Not AI’s To Take campaign, supported by dozens of creative groups representing the recording, writing, publishing, film, television and media industries.

While the government maintains it will not undermine copyright law, the industry minister, Tim Ayres, said on Tuesday “the status quo is no good” for the creative sector, ahead of a package of AI legislation expected by early 2027.

But creatives have pushed back on such claims, arguing copyright law doesn’t need updating – just better enforcement, and that changes could put the $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk.
“[AI platforms] haven’t made one phone call yet. They haven’t called us. They haven’t called anybody,” said Dean Ormston, CEO of music rights organisation Apra Amcos.
“There’s nothing wrong with the copyright framework. The problem is getting somebody to sit at the table and have a discussion with us.”

Not AI’s To Take is backed by the likes of Aria, the Copyright Agency, the Australian Directors’ Guild, Screen Producers Australia, the Australian Society of Authors, the Australian Writers’ Guild, and media organisations including Foxtel, Free TV, Nine, Seven and Guardian Australia.

Australian musicians including Montaigne and KLP have backed the campaign online, while Guardian Australia understands Barnes, Kelly and Garrett – some of Anthony Albanese’s favourite musicians – will also feature.

“Our government has been a huge supporter of Australian music and creativity, and now we’re asking them to continue that support by standing firm on copyright and making sure big tech doesn’t get to rewrite the rules at the expense of creators,” said KLP, real name Kristy Lee Peters.
In quotes shared on the campaign’s website, Barnes said: “I think that these companies should go and f..k themselves.”
Kelly is quoted as saying: “Australia has had some of the best copyright laws, something to be proud of. Now is the time for our government to show some backbone.”

Although Albanese has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law. AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing and training models in Australia, with Anthropic putting forward an “opt-out” model to scrape creative works unless a rightsholder objected.
However Anthropic told a Senate committee it would “provide ongoing access to frontier models to eligible Australian entities, regardless of whether training is permitted.”

The government is expected to unveil a long-awaited legislative package on AI in late 2026 or early 2027, with proposals around datacentres, online safety, productivity and copyright. Albanese said last week that artists “need to be compensated if their work is used”. But the creative community is concerned that lobbying from big tech may sway government decisions.

“This isn’t a smear campaign. We’re just making some noise out in the open, where tech companies are doing it in the shadows,” said Patrizia Di Biase-Dyson, CEO of the Australian Publishers Association.
“Everything is at stake. We have to do as much as possible to educate everyone.”

Ormston said creative industries welcomed the investment and opportunities of AI, and had applauded both Labor’s rebuffing of a text and data mining exemption and Albanese’s public support. But he said artists were worried about potential changes.

“Our very clear message to the government has been: hold firm. You are absolutely saying the right thing. You are absolutely right in the fact that while we want AI in this country, we want it on Australia’s terms,” Ormston said.
Asked about the campaign on Tuesday, Ayres said “nothing has changed in terms of the government’s approach” to copyright.

“I understand the anxiety, though. For those workers, the status quo is no good for them. Their work is currently being appropriated, today, offshore. We have set out a program for a scheme of legislation that would protect those rights, make sure that artificial intelligence investment in Australia is on Australia’s terms.
“We’re not about undermining copyright here. That commitment has been made so many times now.”

A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives, and pledged any copyright changes would “deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
But independent senator David Pocock urged caution around any moves, warning that copyright changes could create a legal “loophole” to make Australia a global “data laundering hotspot”.

“There are more than 100 court cases on foot involving copyright and AI training in the US and we should wait for these to play out before making any changes given the risks of getting it wrong are so high,” he said.

items.title: Chris Minns’ backflips are adding up. Is he ‘clearing the runway’ or panicking?
paragraphs: If recent coverage is to be believed, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, is a talented gymnast. A last-minute intervention by the premier on Monday afternoon, the day before a suite of reforms on underquoting were due to take effect, marks a quadruple or quintuple policy “backflip” by Minns in recent weeks, depending on who you ask.

The laws banning real estate agents from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a previously rejected written offer have been shelved for up to a year, after the premier flagged on Monday morning he had received concerns from estate agents in his own electorate about their effect amid a housing market downturn.
The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the move was “government by 2GB”, referencing the Sydney talkback radio station which had also raised the issue on Monday morning.
“But this isn’t the first time” she told presenter Ben Fordham on Tuesday.
First, the government backed down last month from implementing changes to several local and regional rail line timetables after criticism from commuters.

Next, after a social media post by Sloane, it changed gender-neutral language of “carer” and “lactating parents” in a new parliamentary breastfeeding policy to reflect what Minns said was “commonsense language like ‘mother’ and ‘breastfeeding’”.

After the Daily Telegraph ran a “Nup to the Cup” campaign against plastics legislation, which included requiring cafes to offer dine-in customers mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups, the government dropped the changes, which would not have been implemented until 2028.
This weekend, it made an election promise of a two-year funding guarantee for community preschools after the opposition had warned the sector was facing a $150m annual cut from January.

But Eamonn Fitzpatrick, a lobbyist and former communications and campaign advisor to federal and state Labor governments, says the reversals are more about “clear air” than pre-campaign jitters as the government enters the final sitting days before the March election.
“That is the job of this final sitting week, let’s not forget you go into summer. It’s a dead period,” says Fitzpatrick, who worked alongside Minns in the office of former Labor premier Morris Iemma.
“What you’re seeking to do, actually, in either putting things on hold, changing your minds, revising policies, you’re actually just minimising distraction … clearing the runway.”
Fitzpatrick says interventions are part of Minns’ brand as a strong leader, but insists his style is no more top-down than previous premiers.

Minns has consistently polled ahead of Sloane as preferred premier but he has made no secret about the threat from One Nation, whom he and his ministers have started to refer to as the state’s unofficial opposition.

Peter Lewis, the non-executive chair of strategic communications company Essential, which undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election, said recent polling suggested voting intention in November in NSW was at 27% for Labor, 26% for One Nation and 23% for the Coalition.

Lewis says he thinks the threat of One Nation in NSW is being “used to push the political debate towards the right and could be used as an excuse for the government not to embrace more progressive policies”.

“I wonder if there is a bit of a mistake in that. One Nation voters are being driven by dissatisfaction with the status quo and so governments that are seen as actually addressing issues probably have a better case to answer.”

Defending its underquoting backflip, Labor has said it is protecting buyers from being shut out of sales at lower prices amid a downturn which has seen home values in Sydney drop by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.

In question time, the fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose department was responsible for the reforms and who has now been overruled for a third time by Minns on policy, said the market had changed and the government had responded.
Both he and Minns pointed out that Sloane and the opposition had supported the underquoting laws at the time, which were conceived for a “rising hot market”.
But, Lewis says “there is a cost in being seen to change a position” – and points to Peter Dutton’s 2025 federal election campaign as an example.

“Maybe Minns has done this early enough in the cycle for it not to be an issue, but as you get close to the election it changes, particularly when they’re walking back commitments that have been made to benefit people.

items.title: ‘We don’t want our city to lose its storytellers’: Sydney artists given $25k in Australian first – no strings attached
paragraphs: Julian Hamman feels as if a “great weight” has been lifted from his shoulders. On Monday the 26-year-old film-maker from Sydney was calculating how many more casual shifts he would need to pick up as a gallery host and paramedic assistant in order to finance his creative work.

But on Tuesday night, Hamman found out he is one of 40 creatives to receive an “artist living grant”, a new initiative from the City of Sydney which awards him a catch-free lump sum of $25,000 to simply continue living and working as a creative.

“From my casual jobs I’ve made around $25,000 [this year] and a lot of that goes towards groceries and having to fit my schedule around my work,” he says. “The brain task-switching you do when you work freelance and two jobs is exhausting … Having a base income will allow me to focus on my practice and have some brain space.”

Totalling $1m, the 40 new grants were approved by the council on Monday night, awarding no-strings-attached direct payments not tied to specific projects, based on a successful basic income for artists introduced in Ireland three years ago. Ireland’s pilot scheme was made permanent in February 2026, giving 2,000 creative workers €325 a week.

“Our research shows artists are leaving Sydney due to low incomes, rising costs and limited resources,” Sydney’s lord mayor, Clover Moore, said in a statement. “We don’t want our city to lose its local storytellers and creative soul.
“While it’s not a cure all, these grants will boost 40 Sydney artists working across a range of artforms at different points in their careers, with many from under-represented communities.”

According to Creative Australia’s most recent report, practising professional artists in Australia earned average gross incomes of $54,500 in the 2021–2022 financial year, comprising $23,200 in creative income, $15,300 in arts-related income and $16,000 in non-arts income.
The first of its kind in the country, Sydney’s $25,000 grant is open to artists of all disciplines, from all over the city – not only those who live in the City of Sydney catchment.

Kamilaroi and Tongan musician David Leha, who makes music as Radical Son, is another recipient. He applied for the grant in August and says the money will help with living costs, touring costs and promoting his music.

“It won’t pay for one thing, but it will help with all things,” says the 50-year-old, who is based in Liverpool. “I have been in the arts now for 25 years and it hasn’t been easy, especially in the last decade. There’s a saying that you often have to pay to play and in some cases we’re losing money to perform, so to be able to get this support is really helpful. The costs go on and on.”

Leha splits his time between writing, recording and touring new music and studying for a PhD in creative studies at the University of Newcastle. Along with the rising cost of living, he says the particular challenges he faces as a First Nations musician make it difficult to make enough money from music alone.

“We are expected to have a social media presence and unfortunately some venues are booking based on your following rather than the quality of the music itself, and as First Nations artists our stories are so diverse, but it might not necessarily translate to getting bums on seats.”
Morgan Hogg, a multidisciplinary artist of Cook Island Māori (Ngāti Tāne), Tahitian and English descent, is another recipient of the inaugural grant.
“It’s such a pivotal time in my career,” she says. “I’m about five years into my career as a professional artist and it’ll mean having more time to dedicate to my practice. I’m very grateful.”

The 26-year-old, based in Ashfield, supports her career with a casual job at the Sydney College of the Arts. “Some weeks I’ll work an eight-hour shift, and some days I’ll work 20 hours a week. It depends on how much work they have for me and how much time I need to spend on art projects.”

Hogg estimates she spends 80% of her time as an artist on admin, including identifying and applying for arts grants. “For a project for next year alone I have applied for seven different grants, and I write them all myself … it probably takes me two to three weeks outside of my normal job and I don’t necessarily get paid for it.”

The $25,000 grant, which is expected to be paid to all 40 artists by the end of the year, will help fund Hogg’s travel to the Cook Islands, Tahiti and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for two video works, which involve working with traditional knowledge holders in the region.
The City of Sydney says it will not dictate how the grant money is spent. It can fund any aspect of creative practice, living expenses and the costs of producing new work.

“There are no specific requirements to ‘create’, or restrictions on other work, meaning the money can be spent on … whatever the artist needs,” said City of Sydney Greens councillor Sylvie Ellsmore in a statement. Ellsmore put forward a motion for an artist’s basic income three years ago, which led to this new grant.

“Sydney is losing more artists than any other capital city, because it’s so expensive to live here. Meanwhile too much arts funding is still being allocated to big name, commercial festivals, who often don’t pay artists enough – or at all,” she said.
“Basic income models are how we should be funding the arts – with money going directly to artists, musicians, writers and creators, no strings attached.”

items.title: Night riders: the passengers you meet as a Sydney taxi driver – in pictures
paragraphs: The photojournalist and former taxi driver Glenn Lockitch photographed his passengers between 2003 and 2009 as he drove around Sydney at night, hearing their stories and learning about their lives. ‘Picking up passengers, I became immersed in the ebb and flow of Sydney’s rhythms,’ Lockitch says. ‘The taxi became my photographic studio.’ A selection of these photos are on show in his exhibition TAXI! items.title: Australia’s gender pay gap falls below 20% for first time
paragraphs: Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26.
The Workplace Gender Equality Agency’s (WGEA) report on Wednesday showed men still dominated top-paid positions but businesses’ decisions have narrowed the gap.

Christine Castley, the WGEA’s CEO, said most Australian employers were ignoring backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) measures and improving their hiring and promotion to ensure women reached senior positions.
“Employers are actually thinking in a very deliberate way about what’s going on with workplace gender equality and then taking action,” Castley told Guardian Australia.
The overall WGEA pay gap was 19.7% for the year, with the 2025-26 survey including federal government public sector employers for the first time.
The figure has improved significantly in the last decade, from 26.3% in 2015-16. Coverage has also increased, now covering more than 6 million employees across 9,096 employers.
The private sector’s pay gap fell from 21.1% last year to 20.3% this year, as women accounted for a growing share of full-time management and leadership roles.
Bigger pay rises in female-dominated industries, including retail, aged care and childcare, also helped narrow the gap.
However, women-dominated industries and occupations were still typically paid less than those dominated by men. The average woman still earned $27,467 less per year than the average man, WGEA found.
The survey accounted not only for wages but all earnings, including penalty rates, superannuation, bonuses and overtime. Average total remuneration in the survey was $125,568.
The overall distribution of pay did not improve from 2024-25. Women make up about half of Australia’s workforce but men remained overrepresented in the highest-paid positions.
Every level of management was dominated by men, WGEA found. The disparity was greatest at the chief executive level, where three in four CEOs were men and the gender pay gap widened to 27.6%.

Women accounted for just 36% of employees in the top pay quartile in the private sector. In the commonwealth public sector, women’s representation in the top quartile was 46% and the gender pay gap was just 7.8%.

Promotion rates are similar between genders but women are less represented at higher levels, likely because they resign or take time off for care and domestic responsibilities, previous WGEA work has found.
Wednesday’s report found just 7% of manager roles are part-time, but 29% of women work part-time compared with 12% of men. WGEA called for workplaces to redesign roles to allow more part-time work.
In the financial services sector, which has the worst pay gap at 26.7%, men would be more likely to be promoted or get bonuses as they took on more visible work, Castley said.

“[It’s] the person who can attend the client functions [and] can be available 24/7, the person who’s most visible to the leadership of the organisation, versus, perhaps, the person [doing] the work that’s behind the scenes,” Castley said.
Superannuation provider Rest was an outlier in the finance industry. Its pay gap has fallen to 9.4%, from 20.1% in 2022.

Rest’s chief people officer, Amy Murrell, said the improvements had been helped by extending paid parental leave to all permanent staff, regardless of gender, time of arrival or primary or secondary carer classification.
“It’s not going to happen naturally,” Murrell said. “I think you have to prioritise it for it to make sense.”
The firm had also increased representation after setting targets for at least 40% of employees to be women and 40% men at every level of its business, from its board to its investment team.

Castley said some Australian business leaders had taken on an “anti-DEI” narrative, amid global backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion measures, but most businesses were “getting on with the job”.

WGEA asked businesses to set new targets for the first time in 2026. The most popular goals included improving gender balance at junior and managerial levels and consulting employees on gender equality efforts.

“These are the real issues that need to be tackled … and it’s actually very reassuring that those are the targets that employers have picked because it demonstrates, I think, a very real commitment to actually taking action,” Castley said.

items.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
paragraphs: Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.
The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:
One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.
A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.
A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.
All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.
A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.
Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.
"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."
Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.
Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".
In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."
She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".
When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.
Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."
She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".
"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.
"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."
During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"
Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".
She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."
In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."
