items.title: I gasped at the new Tin Can phone – I’ve been looking for a solution like this for months
paragraphs: Yes, I genuinely gasped when the Tin Can press release landed in my inbox this morning, as it is exactly the product I've been searching for.

While I'm committed to a smartphone-free childhood for my children, I empathise with my children's need to communicate with their friends outside of school. They're also a bit young for the best dumbphones, but I still gatekeep my phone, only allowing occasional texting to other parent's phones in order to reach their pals. And I suddenly realised how unfair this is.

When I was nine, as my daughter is now, I was using our landline to call friends every day, honing valuable communication skills, and the lack of a home phone in my house means that my daughter is unable to do the same. As a new product, it's filling a very real gap in family life – and it's beautifully designed as well.

The Tin Can is already available in the US and Canada, and it's now making it to the UK. It runs on Wi-Fi, so no costly extra landline charges on your broadband (the route I was all set to go down), it looks simple to use, is crucially screen-free, and comes in a variety of delicious colours. It also has helpful parent controls, including restrictions like 'quiet time', you can only call other Tin Can handsets (for free), as well as parent-approved numbers (as part of a monthly subscription), and emergency numbers.
Of course, for best results, your children's friends also need to have a Tin Can – so I'm off to convince the parents I know to put it on their Christmas lists.
Pre orders are open for the UK, and it will arrive with you from 30 November.

items.title: Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036
paragraphs: Alan Milburn's long-awaited plan to help young people who are neither learning nor earning promises to save money from the UK's welfare bill.

Milburn said he believes his proposed reforms, which would reduce benefits for some young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neets) but aim to get them jobs in the long run, could save as much as £13.8bn in welfare costs over the next 10 years.

But after the extra spending he has proposed for job guarantees from the government, hiring incentives for firms, and health and education support, his reforms are only projected to save £200m a year of taxpayers' money overall by 2036.
BBC Verify has taken a look through the numbers.
Analysts have expressed concerns about the sharply rising number of young people claiming health and disability benefits in recent years.

The Milburn report estimates that around £8bn a year is currently being spent on benefits directly for young people through the welfare system, made up of £4.6bn on Universal Credit and £3.2bn on Personal independence payments (Pip).

The number of 16-24 year olds in England and Wales claiming the health element of Universal Credit has increased from 105,000 in 2020 to 193,000 this year according to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).
Young Pip claimants have also increased from 230,000 to 511,000 over that time, while official forecasts suggest this number is set to rise, external above 800,000 by 2037.
Milburn's reforms would combine two major policies in relation to young people:
A significant increase in government spending to help them into employment and training
Reductions in the welfare payments available to some of the group
Milburn's long-term plans call for an additional £5.8bn in spending per year by 2036 on things such as employment subsidies and mental health support to help get young people into work or education.

He is also proposing a new benefits system so young people would not be able to access the same kind of health and disability benefits as older people, including creating a Youth Allowance instead of giving under-25s Universal Credit and a new Additional Cost Allowance that could replace Pip benefits.

Milburn estimates that these reforms would contribute to a reduction of total welfare spending of £3.6bn a year by 2036 relative to where spending would otherwise have been in that year, and said it could save a cumulative £13.8bn from the welfare bill over the next decade.

Milburn said his diagnosis applies UK-wide, but education, skills, health and local government are devolved to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. He has called on the devolved administrations to agree "a shared set of headline outcomes".

Official forecasts show the total welfare system, external is projected to cost £353bn this year. There is no official forecast of the level of total welfare spending in 2036, but likely inflation means it would be above the £431bn currently projected for 2032.

Around half of this cost is the state pension, on which spending is forecast to rise from £154bn a year to £193bn a year. Spending on Pip and disability living allowance are also set to rise over that time from £40bn a year to £57bn a year.
However, as a share of the overall economy, the increase in the cost of the welfare system is less dramatic.
Total welfare spending is forecast to rise from 11.1% of GDP this year to 11.3% in 2032. This would be below the the peak of around 12% seen in 2013 following the global financial crisis.
That has led some economists and researchers to question the argument, external that welfare spending is out of control.
The reductions touted as part of Milburn's reforms, if delivered, is likely to only reduce the UK's benefits bill by a relatively small amount.
As a share of today's welfare bill, the £3.6bn of annual savings in 2036 would be only 1%.

As well as the £5.8bn that would be spent on supporting young people into work, training or college, Milburn estimates the government would reap £2.4bn a year in additional taxes, as more people would be in work.
This £2.4bn of additional taxes combined with the £3.6bn in lower welfare spending would add up to £6bn a year in 2036.
That implies a net saving for the government as a result of Milburn's proposed package of £200m by that year, although this saving would grow over time.
The £200m net savings figure in the Milburn report is also in today's money - and would be larger in cash terms in 2036, though the actual cash figure will depend on inflation over the next decade.
Additional reporting by Tom Edginton and data journalism by Christine Jeavans

items.title: Batman to James Bond: The clues about what to expect from Robert Pattinson's 007
paragraphs: He has been in big-budget blockbusters like Twilight, Tenet and The Batman, as well as a string of quirky arthouse films - so what clues can Robert Pattinson's past roles give us about what he might be like as James Bond?
Every actor creates a new James Bond, and Pattinson is one of the best in the business at crafting a memorable character.
The British actor can be an action man or an anti-hero, a romantic lead or a comic fool. He can be granite-faced or goofy, and everything in between.
"I was thinking about what the aspects of James Bond are, and he's done all of those throughout his career," says Paul Tweddle, host of the Heavy Spoilers film podcast, external.

He cites Pattinson's performance as a brooding heartthrob in teen vampire franchise Twilight, his suave and quick-witted secret agent in Christopher Nolan's Tenet, the withdrawn and focused title character in The Batman, and the ruthless and manipulative Antinous in Nolan's The Odyssey.
Pattinson has "often been drawn to really dark fare", says Anna Smith, film critic and host of the Girls on Film podcast, external.

"Wouldn't it be interesting to see Bond go a little bit darker?" she suggested to the BBC's World Service. "But also what he's got, and I'd like him to do more of, is comedy. And goodness knows, we need a Bond who can handle humour."
Unusually for a James Bond actor, one word that has cropped up frequently is "weird".
Earlier this month, Pattinson was described as "the weirdest guy in Hollywood" by the Celebrating Cinema podcast, external.
"Pattinson is an actor who makes bold, interesting, risky choices. For such a handsome guy, he can bring the weird, and then some," wrote Chris Hewitt in Empire, external.
"About 0.07 seconds after the announcement, people were already anticipating the weird with his Bond. And they may well get their wish."
Pattinson (right) starred with Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse in 2019

Variety's chief critic Guy Lodge said, external Pattinson's reputation as an actor "has been considerably enriched by his predilection for playing, frankly, losers and weirdos", such as in more offbeat films like Good Time, The Lighthouse, Primetime and Mickey 17.

"Even his blockbuster assignments are more interesting when he lets his inner freak out to play," Lodge added. "His big, heightened, leeringly villainous turn in The Odyssey is off on its own beam entirely."
Associated Press film critic Jake Coyle said, external smaller films like The Lighthouse and High Life show "Pattinson's proclivity for pushing boundaries".

"He's certainly the funniest and quickest to laugh James Bond we've had in decades," Coyle continued. "It will be interesting to see how much of his personality bleeds into Bond, or how much the tux stifles it."
So what do Pattinson's performances in some of his biggest films tell us about what to expect?
Pattinson in Tenet with Himesh Patel (left) and John David Washington (right)
Pattinson plays a dapper and enigmatic British agent in Christopher Nolan's time-bending 2020 thriller, as adept at bungeeing off an arms dealer's tower as he is delivering some deliciously dry wit.
"He's very suave, he's thinking on his feet," Tweddle says. "He's someone who's holding his cards close to his chest and not necessarily giving the game away.
"Tenet is the obvious one where Nolan's basically doing a kind of James Bond movie."

The Times' chief critic Kevin Maher agrees, external: "Pattinson has effectively played Bond already, when he effortlessly inhabited the role of the suave yet nonetheless lethal British spy Neil in Tenet.
"For many observers (including this one) that was the role. That was the audition. There was no turning back after Neil."

New York Times critic Alissa Wilkinson noted that Pattinson has picked up other "Bond-adjacent" roles. "The most obvious is Bruce Wayne, a.k.a. Batman, the wealthy playboy with a lair of tech toys and his own gussied-up automobile," she wrote, external.
"Wayne and Bond have a lot in common on paper, but in Pattinson's hands Wayne becomes emo, reclusive, awkward, with the hair of a '90s grunge rocker."

The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw also pointed out, external parallels with how Pattinson played "the darkly conflicted caped crusader Batman in Matt Reeves's 2022 film, lurking athletically in the shadows - like Bond, used to working in secret".
Like Tenet, The Batman proved Pattinson is an expert at action scenes, whether that be jumping off a building or being involved in an explosive car chase with The Penguin.
"Batman is a really good example of where he's a withdrawn figure, someone who has his mind focused solely on a task, and I think that's a big part of what James Bond needs to be," Tweddle says.
However, Pattinson's 007 should be a little less brooding and aloof than his stony-faced Batman and Bruce Wayne.
Although Pattinson plays the villain in Nolan's Greek epic, Antinous's menace and ruthlessness could come in handy when playing Bond, according to Tweddle.
"I think Robert Pattinson also has quite a psychotic side to him, which a lot of the James Bond books delve into - how he's a killer, and he needs to have that side to him," he says.
"What he's done in The Odyssey shows he can be manipulative, and connive and make certain plans, which is what a spy needs to do."
Collider's Collier Jennings named, external The Odyssey, along with Tenet and The Batman, as films that show Pattinson is "the perfect" fit for Bond.
"All three roles carry an element that makes James Bond work," Jennings wrote.
"Batman has the combat skills and subterfuge you'd need to be a spy of Bond's caliber, not to mention the cutting edge hardware.
"Neil has a great grasp on the intricacies of pulling off complex covert operations.
"Antonius walks with a swagger and arrogance that either makes you love him or hate him."
Pattinson's current film sees him play real-life NBC journalist Chris Hansen, who carried out sting operations on suspected paedophiles for TV show To Catch a Predator.
It again demonstrates Pattinson's range as an actor and his ability to take on complex roles - he balances the portrayal of Hansen not as a villain but equally not as a hero.
"He's very much face-to-face with the predators in the room, and he's controlling the situation," Tweddle explains.

"It's very confrontational and demands a certain amount of power. Being able to control the room like that is also quite transferable to James Bond, and interrogations are a big part of what he does."
Pattinson will next be seen playing shape-shifting villain Scytale in the forthcoming third instalment of the epic sci-fi series - directed by Denis Villeneuve.
The pair's reunion for the next Bond movie is not a coincidence. Villeneuve's experience of working with Pattinson on the film may have been the deciding factor when casting James Bond.

"The thing I adore with Robert Pattinson is that when you roll cameras, there's always a certain moment where you have no idea what will happen. He is an explosion in front of the camera," the director told Time, external before the Bond casting was announced.
"He has an incredible imagination and is a very playful actor, and a very creative actor, always trying to bring new ways of expressing himself and always trying to surprise me."
Surprising, bold, weird? One thing is for certain, Pattinson's James Bond is going to be interesting.

items.title: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
paragraphs: Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the attack, though he is yet to comment.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The Security Service of Ukraine said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
paragraphs: The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.

The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.
When a company floats it issues a prospectus for would-be investors that details its activities and lays out the share offering, including an estimated price.

Anthropic’s prospectus explains that the shares on sale will be 825m of class A common stock, and that the initial public offering (IPO) price will between $70 and $78 a share. However, the final price will be set on Wednesday.

The shares will come with voting rights, but, if all the shares’ votes are combined they will only represent 49.9% of the total vote available, so will not allow buyers to be able to force any changes in the way the company is run.
The shares will be listed on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday, and will be available to individual investors alongside big institutions.

In the UK, several investment platforms are offering customers the chance to subscribe to shares, including AJ Bell, Hargreaves Lansdown, Robinhood and eToro. At Robinhood and eToro the minimum investment is $250 (£189), at Hargreaves Lansdown the minimum investment is £250, and at AJ Bell investors will need at least £1,000 to apply. AJ Bell is closing applications at 1pm on Wednesday, while Hargreaves Lansdown and Robinhood will close at 3pm. All say they could close the doors early without notice.
Once the IPO has happened and the shares have been listed they can be bought at any point, and through platforms that have not been involved in the IPO.

Yes – in fact, there are already funds which own stakes in the company. In the UK they include the Baillie Gifford US Growth and Scottish Mortgage investment trusts, while Fidelity has investments held in funds available to US investors.

Once the IPO is over, the stock will ultimately find its way into some tracker funds – although some will be quicker than others – and managers of actively invested funds could also choose to buy shares. That means people might well end up investing in Anthropic even if they do not attempt to buy any shares directly.
Anthropic’s prospectus includes 92 pages on potential risks to the company and its industry, so it is not an investment for the faint-hearted.
Recent weeks have highlighted the fragility of the US markets, and tech stocks in particular, so this is one to consider very carefully.

Nils Pratley, the Guardian’s financial editor, has raised questions about the company’s governance structure, saying it “represents an extraordinary concentration of power in the hands of a few individuals”.
Jason Hollands, the managing director of the investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners – which is not participating in the IPO – highlights some other things investors need to consider.

“Anthropic would give most retail investors the first opportunity to have a direct stake in a frontier AI developer. But it remains a capital-intensive business, and it has yet to establish a consistent path to profitability,” he says. “Investors will need to judge whether the company can turn demand for its models into durable earnings.”
Hollands says if demand for shares exceeds the limited supply, “that could support the price initially with a ‘pop’, but it does not guarantee a strong debut or lasting gains over the coming months”.

He adds the SpaceX listing in June “is a reminder that a hotly anticipated IPO and early enthusiasm can quickly be followed by volatility: its shares have traded below their IPO price at points since listing”.

When we asked Claude whether to buy shares in Anthropic it was upfront about why it is not a great source of investment advice: “I can’t tell you whether you should buy. I’m not a financial adviser, and I’m also made by Anthropic, so I have an obvious conflict of interest here.”

It went on to present a few facts about the IPO, and some useful questions that any investor should be considering before buying an individual share in an IPO. Can you cope with a loss if it goes down in value? How much of your portfolio will an investment in it represent? Will you already have exposure to the share through a tracker fund?

items.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
paragraphs: For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag.

Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck.

Keepsake County also takes inspiration from the popular extraction shooter genre, which sees you dropping into a map and trying to get out with sackfuls of loot. But you don’t kill anyone in Keepsake County – you merely tie pesky proprietors up with bits of lace lifted from old trainers. Nor do you use your hard-earned stash to craft upgrades. Rather, it’s straight to the pawn shop with each haul.

Quickly, I found a pleasant groove, slipping into houses and robbing each owner blind. I would find an appropriate point of entry, fiddle with the locks, and then get to thieving work, carefully evading various residents such as teen babysitters and retired boomers. Over time, as I discovered more elements of lead character Samuel’s debt-ridden backstory, the break-ins began to feel a little more tragic, as if the only way he might experience a more comfortable life is as a voyeur in these massive houses. The loading screens – shots of empty, pastoral countryside as if viewed from the side window of his dilapidated car – reinforce the melancholy. What a hard, lonely existence.

The story is artfully told, economically relayed, simultaneously a satire of nowheresville suburban culture and an earthy, acid-tinged love letter to the midwest (and would surely make a nice complement to whatever Grand Theft Auto VI has to say about the US in a few days). Yet you can feel where the tiny DIY team, Forward Instinct, has compromised. I came across repeated lines of dialogue from a diner waitress, while the visual distinctions of each region (including plains and backwoods) do little to impact how the game plays. And while aspects of the levels, including item locations and building architecture, are remixed every time you load them up, the action can begin to feel a little one note, as if you’re stealing from the same house over and over.

But Keepsake County also derives a great deal of bite from such monotony. You come to realise that Samuel has no chance of paying off his medical debts and legal fees. Financially, his situation is hopeless. And so, with little possibility of getting into the black, these robberies take on a nihilistic bent – our antihero has nothing left to lose. Yet Keepsake County is not wholly despairing even as it shows how undignified day-to-day survival in America can be. There is a youthful, delinquent charm to this game: one moment you are bribing a guard dog with a juicy bone, the next you are stealing homeware from someone so comparatively rich they might never even notice it’s gone.

items.title: Ukraine hails attack on vital Kerch bridge linking Russia and Crimea – Europe live
paragraphs: Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.
Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.
The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.
The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.
Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.
Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.
They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.
It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Serbia's new deputies take seats in parliament after landmark Student List win
Biden's memoir uncovers his views on Zelenskyy, Ukraine, Macron, Brexit
Thursday's Ukraine talks 'very important' to get structure of peace negotiations right, Stubb says
Hungary suspends rail traffic to Ukraine after Russian drone hits railway station near border
France's Le Pen vows to repeal Macron's pension reform, bring down retirement age
'Trust has been restored' after crisis talks to save Dutch coalition government, PM Jetten says
Kremlin says Kerch bridge will be rebuilt 'even better' after Ukrainian strike
Germany's Merz hosts Finland's Stubb for discussions on Ukraine ahead of key talks on Thursday
Zelenskyy hails 'unprecedented operation' that led to strike against Kerch Bridge
46 injured, four seriously, in train crash in Prague
'Europe needs to wake up' to realise defence costs if Ukraine fails, Danish minister says
Germany to contribute $300m for US air defence systems for Ukraine ahead of 'exceptionally difficult winter', Pistorius says
Morning opening: Ukraine hits crucial bridge linking Russia and Crimea

The 140 successful candidates from Serbia’s Student List have just been sworn in as MPs at the National Assembly in Belgrade. They took the oath en masse, alongside members of the long-governing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which now finds itself in opposition for the first time in 14 years.

It follows the spectacular triumph of the Student List in last month’s parliamentary elections. It comfortably defeated the SNS and its populist leader Aleksandar Vučić with a slate of candidates drawn from academia, athletics and economics, among other disciplines. None of the new MPs have any political experience.

Before the parliamentary session, Student List supporters gathered outside the National Assembly to cheer their representatives. Some of them performed the traditional kolo circle dance in celebration.

Meanwhile, there were jeers and whistles for arrivals from Vučić’s party. A woman in the crowd poured a bottle of drinking yoghurt over the head of SNS candidate Lidija Vukićević, who said she felt “very bad” about the “primitivism and vulgarity” of Student List supporters.

Now the MPs have been sworn in, the next task is to elect a parliamentary speaker. Whoever it is become the acting president of Serbia – because Vučić resigned as head of state to make his unsuccessful attempt to become prime minister.
Separately, former US president Joe Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, got published today, and it features some interesting lines on European affairs.

Just skimming the book for now, there is a bit of interesting background on the US response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and his secret visit to Kyiv in February 2023, as well as some of Biden’s unfiltered views on Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“But I must admit that it could be difficult to work with Zelensky[y]. As brave as he and the Ukrainians were, they tested our patience on many occasions, demanding more armaments and money. …

Zelensky[y] could be moody and stubborn in our private conversations, and not as grateful as I would have expected. That could be frustrating, and I let him know that in no uncertain terms. Still, I refused to cut and run on the Ukrainians, who possessed a tremendous fighting spirit. And so did Zelensky[y].”

In longer paragraphs on Ukraine, Biden writes he was “not blind to Ukraine’s faults,” including “too much corruption” in the country’s judicial system, “where the rich and powerful were often free to buy their way out of accountability.” “Ukraine would have to deal with these challenges if they wanted genuine integration with Europe and the West.”

“But I had also seen the inner strength of the Ukrainian people. They deserved a fighting chance. If they could create a real democracy, with checks and balances, and fair elections, they could be a bulwark in the region, and an inspiration to peoples everywhere who were trying to claw their way out of a history of repression.”
He also reveals that Donald Trump’s transition team after the 2024 elections wanted to get a permission to immediately start negotiations with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

“During the transition, Donald Trump’s team had asked me to sign a letter empowering them to negotiate directly with Putin, even before he took office. But I refused, unwilling to give them carte blanche for what I expected would be a kind of surrender, at Ukraine’s expense.”

Elsewhere, Biden also writes about his relationships with other leaders, including first foreign trip as president, to attend a G7 summit in Cornwall in 2021, noting his “bittersweet” feelings about “saying goodbye to an old friend, Angela Merkel,” while remarking how “impressed” he was by France’s Emmanuel Macron.
“[He] enthusiastically welcomed me into the group, but he asked hard questions about the rise of populism in the United States and how it might affect our long-term foreign policy.”
double quotation mark“When I said, ‘America’s back,’ he responded, ‘For how long?’”

Writing about Brexit, Biden – who is of Irish heritage on his mother’s side – expresses his frustration that the withdrawal from the EU was “threatening to undermine the Good Friday agreement of 1998, which had done so much good in bringing peace to Northern Ireland.”

“I also disapproved of Brexit for its ultranationalist claims, and for making many promises that could not possibly be kept. I believed that the populist leaders and opportunists who backed Brexit had sold the British people a false bill of goods.”
Finland’s Alexander Stubb just addressed reporters in Berlin, after meeting Germany’s president Frank-Walter Steinmeier.
Stubb said the upcoming meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday will be “very important” for the peace process.
“I think it’s important that we get a structure and order in the negotiations, which basically means that there’s a clear timetable and that there’s a clear agenda.”

“The process is not going to be fast, but I think it should be well structured. … I think the key here is that you cannot speak about territory without Ukraine. You cannot speak about security without Europe.”
Stubb also explained his approach to engagement with Russia, rooted in three key issues: geography, diplomacy and military.

“We need diplomacy. If you don’t talk about peace, you will never get peace. And in order to be able to get peace, you need to have dialogue and conversation and diplomacy. … We believe that in order for you to have a diplomatic say in the geographic situation that you are in, you have to back it up with something.”
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles hit the Northern and Southern bridges – two major transport arteries that cross the Dnipro river.
Traffic was also suspended, causing gridlock early on Tuesday morning.
Russia’s army confirmed it had hit both bridges in a “massive attack” on Ukraine’s infrastructure, AFP reported.

Hungary will suspend rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days after a Russian drone struck just hundreds of meters from a railway station in western Ukraine, Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar said.
“Recently, in Transcarpathia, a Russian drone struck 300 meters from the Mukachevo railway station.
The Hungarian crew of the train arriving from Hungary has been taken off the train.
We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for today and tomorrow.”
Mukachevo is just across the Hungarian-Ukrainian border on the Ukrainian side, in an area inhabited by many ethnic Hungarians.
Hungary’s foreign minister Anita Orbán – no link with that Orbán – offered a bit more detail on the incident.
“At around 10am Hungarian time, Russian Geran-2 drones attacked Transcarpathia in three waves, primarily targeting the areas around Mukachevo and Uzhhorod.

Ukrainian air defence forces responded effectively and shot down several of the attacking drones. Unfortunately, reports have also come in of multiple drone strikes, and the extent of the damage is currently being assessed.

This is not the first air attack against Transcarpathia, and unfortunately it is unlikely to be the last. As Russia intensifies its attacks against Ukraine’s civilian population, we can expect further attacks of this kind against Transcarpathia as well, which until now has been relatively protected due to its geographical location.

Ukraine’s civilian population is likely to face the most difficult winter of the war so far. The electricity grid and district heating systems are already in critical condition, particularly in Kyiv, Kharkiv and southern Ukraine. Russia is expected to intensify its attacks on power generation. Without electricity, water supplies in cities are also disrupted, millions of people are left without heating and power, and everyday life becomes increasingly difficult.

I express my solidarity with the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia and with the entire Ukrainian people, who have now had to face the horrors of war every day for nearly five years and are making extraordinary efforts simply to get through daily life.”
Let’s quickly go back to Ukraine for some news from Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar.
French ⁠far-right leader Marine Le Pen vowed to ​repeal President Emmanuel Macron’s pension ⁠reform if she is elected ⁠next spring and ​bring ‌down the retirement ‌age to 60 ‌to 62.
She also set out plans to create a fund worth €900bn ($990.54bn) to help fund ​pensions in the long term, she added. It ⁠would take a generation ​to ​build up ​the fund, ​she added.
RN President Jordan ​Bardella has said ​the party wants to tighten the rules governing pension contribution periods and encourage employers to keep older workers in jobs for longer.
On Friday, we reported on crisis talks aimed at saving Rob Jetten’s three-party minority government in the Netherlands.

The crisis erupted late last week when lawmakers from D66 and the Christian Democrats brokered a deal with center-left opposition parties in parliament to pass a contentious tax package, angering the third coalition partner. AP reported.
But it looks like they have managed to agree on a new way forward, with Jetten announcing a fresh start for the coalition bitterly divided by last week’s tax plans.

“We realise that we have tested the patience of the entire nation, but we are also relieved that, following several days of constructive discussions within the Cabinet and the coalition, trust has been restored,” Jetten said. “In doing so, we have laid the foundation to continue working together in this current composition.”
Let’s take a quick look at other news from across Europe.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin said its bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia will be “even better” after it is rebuilt following a large-scale Ukrainian attack that caused significant damage.
“There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.
Finland’s highly influential president Alexander Stubb has arrived in Berlin this morning for talks with Germany’s Friedrich Merz.

The pair meets just two days before the highly anticipated threeway talks between US president Donald Trump, China president Xi Jinping, and Russia president Vladimir Putin in Manila and an ‘unprecedented’ meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday.

The Berlin meeting is expected to bring together over 30 national leaders, including Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the two US peace envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who will be able to brief European partners on the Manila talks held a few hours earlier, Politico Berlin Playbook reported.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has hailed the strike against the Kerch Bridge as “an unprecedented operation” with direct consequences “for the primary military supply route connecting Russian territory to our Ukrainian Crimea.”
He said it was “the seventh phase of an operation that has been under way for several weeks,” with “systematic” destruction of air defence systems, radar and other electronic warfare assets.

“We have repeatedly proposed de-escalation measures to Russia, yet every such proposal has been met only with emphatic rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure daily – including bridges – in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region.

We are restoring our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capacity is and will remain high, and we will never leave terror against our cities and our people unanswered.”
I am also keeping an eye on an incident in the Czech capital of Prague where two commuter trains collided near the main train station, leaving 46 injured, including four seriously.
The two passenger trains collided on an overpass while travelling at a low speed around 7am this morning, according to the Czech media.
Czech transport minister called it “a very serious” incident, but said the focus was on caring for all affected.
At 10am Czech time, the city’s emergency services said the situation was contained, with all injured transported to hospitals.
Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus has warned that “Europe needs to wake up” as “the price, if Ukraine falls, will be lot higher than the amount we are now delivering for Ukraine.”
“Ukraine has the most efficient and also modern army in all of Europe. We are gaining a lot of advantages [from] the cooperation with the Ukrainians,” he said.
But he added that “the cost of Ukraine losing will be a lot higher” than any current aid given to Kyiv.

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Ukraine is facing “an exceptionally difficult winter” amid intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure as he confirmed Germany will fund a new package of air defence systems for Kyiv.

“Ukraine is facing an exceptionally difficult winter as Russia is doing everything in its power - and will continue to do so – to destroy Ukraine’s water, electricity and energy infrastructure,” he said.
Pistorius said that Russia was “intensifying its aerial assaults because its if failing to make progress on the battlefields.”
“For us, as nations supporting Ukraine, this means one thing clearly: we must continue to provide effective and rapid support for Ukraine’s air defence,” he said.
Germany will contribute $300m for another round of defensive weapons purchases from the US, with Norway also expected to join.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is about far more than solidarity or assisting a nation under attack; it is about the security of Europe – and, by extension, about stopping Putin and keeping him in check.”
During the Ukraine defence contact group, which Pistorius co-chairs, the EU ministers will be joined by the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby.
“This is important, as we have several matters to discuss – for instance, the upcoming Force Posture Review, as well as cooperation on defence equipment and various other topics.”
Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.
Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.
The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.
The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.
Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.
Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.
They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.
It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

items.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
paragraphs: The UK has sanctioned companies it said were involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of settlement goods and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

items.title: Dezeen launches 20x20 project to identify the architects and designers to watch over the next 20 years
paragraphs: Today is Dezeen’s 20th birthday, and to celebrate we launch our 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. For the series we’ve asked 20 architects and designers who have had a major impact over the past 20 years to each select an architect or designer that they believe will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years.
Called 20×20, the project aims to celebrate the past 20 years of Dezeen while looking forward to the names and faces we’ll be seeing much more of in the next 20 years.
We’ll be revealing the selected architects and designers on Dezeen over the next four weeks, getting to know them and their work in a series of interviews.
The series launches today with a profile of Russian-born, Paris-based designer Harry Nuriev, who was selected by Danish architect Bjarke Ingels.

He will be followed by the selections of Es Devlin, Faye Toogood, Francine Houbine, Frida Escobedo, Huberto Campana, Iris van herpen, Jeanne Gang, Kelly Wearstler, Lesley Lokko, Ma Yansong, Marc Newson, Mariam Kamara, Marina Tabassum, Nendo, Neri&Hu, Patricia Urquiola, Philippe Starck, Sabine Marcelis, Sou Fujimoto and Yasmeen Lari.
All of the interviews will be listed below as they are published:

items.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
paragraphs: Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky, Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy.

How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes? This may be due to relevant works being difficult to obtain; for the segment representing Jean Cocteau’s exhibition in January 1938 we have one of his ink drawings for his 1937 play Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, and another in reproduction only.

Kandinsky’s knockout Dominant Curve, we are told, was purchased by Guggenheim directly from its 1938 retrospective appearance, but what of the other, wonderful, Kandinskys also present? His ectoplasmic Green Figure of 1936 is loaned from the Pompidou: was it at Guggenheim Jeune or not? The same may be said of the magnificent – and massive – Mondrian Composition No 1 with Grey and Red 1938 and Composition with Red 1939, explicitly stated as included in the Exhibition of Abstract and Concrete Art in May 1939 and then acquired by Guggenheim for her collection. It’s shown next to César Domela’s Relief no 11 C, a light relief of painted wood and concentric ellipses and honeycomb textures, which by contrast has no contextual anchoring in its text. If an exhibition deliberately cites a prior one, accuracy is crucial. One is inclined to be forgiving however with the inclusion of such rare treats as a tiny 1931 Salvador Dalí, and the barely visible oil on board Old Man Running completed by Lucian Freud apparently aged 15.

In contrast with a previous show at Petersfield Art Gallery about Guggenheim’s time living in West Sussex, which more heavily focused on her social life and affairs, this show is more academically flavoured and less is expounded on her social networking and activities, though they are inextricably bound. The clue is in the show’s subtitle: “the making of a collector” not curator. As such, we glean a sense of Guggenheim as facilitator and promoter of existing players moving within her orbit rather than a visionary selector. She famously set a goal to buy a picture a day, which sounds not unlike someone declaring themselves an intellectual for owning a large library. It was actually Winifred “Wyn” Henderson who managed the gallery, deciding on the name, finding the Cork Street location, shaping its promotional graphic design and using her professional network to bring artists into its circle; and Marcel Duchamp behind the scenes shaping its opening, educating Peggy on the difference between abstraction and surrealism.

We have then among big names that are well established in the art historical canon – Tanguy, represented here beautifully in dreamlike biomorphic landscapes, is said to have been Guggenheim Jeune’s only commercially successful show – lesser known surrealists such as Grace Pailthorpe and Reuben Mednikoff, who were suggested by Wyn and perpetuated what they called “psychorealism”: a mix of automatic drawing with psychoanalysis. Similarly, probably the only reason a sequence of monosyllabic portraits by Cedric Morris were exhibited, featuring the same flat modelling and blank expression, was because he was friends with Guggenheim and delivered a hundred of them to the gallery, of which mercifully only a handful make it here. A revelation however is Wolfgang Paalen’s delightful, macabre umbrella made of sponges, experiments with candle smoke and a gun made out of “poultry and mammal bones, brass and velvet”, mounted so high you’d be forgiven for missing it.

The show was pitched by the Peggy Guggenheim Collection Venice curator Gražina Subelytė and independent curator Simon Grant, so it is useful to bear in mind an underlying purpose serving the Guggenheim estate; it would be instructive to be able to compare Guggenheim Jeune’s purported influence on London contemporary art with other players – such as the Redfern Gallery or Mayor Gallery – beyond such amusing anecdotes cited here that customs were so flummoxed by avant garde art that it was demanded it be imported according to its base materials. Making tangible and cohesive a short but brilliant burst of activity, a precursor to what is now a cultural behemoth in Venice, was clearly a feat enough.
Peggy Guggenheim in London: The Making of a Collector is at the Royal Academy, London, 21 November to 14 March

items.title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-153950/nx-s1-mx-6043667-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.

A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. Adam Gray/Getty Images North America hide caption

President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.

Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027. Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.
Dressed in costumes for Halloween, students of Kids Campus SFCC play at the playground in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative.
Dressed in costumes for Halloween, students of Kids Campus SFCC play at the playground in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape.
Robert Pattinson attends the world premiere of The Odyssey in London in July. Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Europe hide caption
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

items.title: Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
paragraphs: BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the Russian-born, Paris-based architect and designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.
Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.
“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

“Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”
“I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”
“You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen.
Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.
“When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he said. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”
“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”
At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

“Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he said. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”
“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.
“[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”
Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.
“It was really a big experiment,” he said. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.
“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”

Much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.
“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he said.
“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.
“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”
His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

“It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he said. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”

“I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”

The competition to create something new and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.
“[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he said. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”
“I’m trying to find new materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.
“It’s like music – every year there is new songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”
After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.
“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he said. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”
“You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”
He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.
“I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in big development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev says these projects can be the most creative.

“The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he said. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”
“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”

Nuriev believes his most important role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was launched with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.
“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he said.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”
His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.
“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”
“As Coco Chanel said, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.
Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated

items.title: Giant lunar sculpture has visitors over the moon
paragraphs: The Moon sculpture is hanging at the St Helier Methodist Centre
People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.

Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
Eva, nine, said it was "cool" to see a sculpture of the Moon up close
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir.
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.

"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."
Follow BBC Jersey on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to channel.islands@bbc.co.uk, external.

items.title: NHS data contract to stay with Palantir until 2029
paragraphs: The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used.
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

items.title: Sen. Jack Reed says FAA needs a real plan, not just more money
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6042514/nx-s1-10007802" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., attends a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in Washington on April 30, 2026. Graeme Sloan/Getty Images hide caption
After last week's nationwide ground stop, Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., raised concerns Tuesday about the Federal Aviation Administration's oversight of contractors.
"Was the contractor properly supervised? I have questions too about whether FAA, after DOGE, is capable of supervising these types of activities," Reed told NPR's Michel Martin on Morning Edition.
Reed said the administration's explanation of an apparent contractor error made sense, but called for a closer examination of its cause.

Friday's four-hour ground stop occurred as a federal contractor was replacing copper wiring with fiber optic cables at an FAA facility in Arkansas. The exact cause remains under investigation, and federal officials say there is no indication of a cyberattack.
The disruption has renewed debate in Congress over funding for the aging system.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially requested $30 billion in additional funding before increasing the figure to $50 billion. Congress has already provided $14.5 billion for FAA modernization. Roughly $9 billion is still unspent.
Reed, who sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, criticized the administration for seeking more money without presenting a detailed plan.
"They're just trying to throw money at a problem," he said.
Reed also agreed with Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who has questioned whether some of the proposed funding would go toward airport improvements rather than safety.
"The top priority in my book is getting this system back up to speed," Reed said.
Listen to the full interview using the blue button above. This story was adapted for digital by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

items.title: Maybelline's new slogan is a crime against copywriting
paragraphs: Normally it's a visual rebrand that gets hackles raised online. A new logo can draw furious ire, as brands like Jaguar and Cracker Barrel have discovered in recent years. Less controversial tends to be copywriting tweaks. But beauty brand Maybelline's 'new' slogan has infuriated me more. Than. Any. Other. Rebrand. This. Year.

“Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline," was one of the most famous jingles on TV for a while. It first debuted in the 1990s (see the original below), and is burned onto the consciousness of countless viewers. But now, in a attempt to remove its so-called "ambiguity", the slogan has been updated. Nay, butchered. One of the best pieces of copywriting, this ain't.

The new slogan reads: "Maybe. We’re born with it. Maybe. It’s Maybelline." Yes, "she's" has been changed to a more inclusive "we're". But it's that stuttering punctuation that's bothering me. Why does it suddenly sound like it's being recited by somebody struggling to walk up a hill?

According to Sandrine Jolly, Maybelline's global brand president, the original jingle "was giving ambiguity – it was more of a question". Well, yes. That was rather the point. The word 'Maybe' is, by its very nature, an ambiguous word. Its synonyms include 'possibly' or 'perhaps'. Its entire meaning is uncertainty. You can't change that by giving it a full stop. Trying to remove the ambiguity from a slogan built entirely around ambiguity is a bit like changing Nike's 'Just Do It' to 'Please. Consider. Doing. It.'
Maybe. We're Born With It. Welcome to the beauty of infinite possibility. - YouTube

And there's nothing wrong with changing 'she' to 'we'. It's a perfectly reasonable attempt at inclusivity, and one that could have been achieved without completely murdering the rhythm. Instead, Maybelline has taken one of the catchiest jingles of all time and made it sound like a hostage reading out a statement. Four sentences where there used to be two. Does that really make for more certainty?

What makes it all so infuriating is that this feels like change for change's sake. The original slogan was clever, memorable and instantly recognisable. The new one needs an entire press release to explain what its punctuation represents. In an era when brands are realising the importance of their heritage branding assets, maybe, just maybe, Maybelline should have left its slogan. Alone.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?
paragraphs: A cash cow. Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac hide caption
Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac

Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?

Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.
" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money. By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.
Then Google vice president of search Marissa Mayer in 2009. ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images/AFP hide caption

That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion. That's more than a millionfold increase.

Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.

In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.
For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.
But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.

Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer, a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.

Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."

Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.
