items.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
paragraphs: Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation.
An open letter, which has more than 165,000 signatories, demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two big shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

In Washington, however, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next CEO. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.

Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing, Alice Huang.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to China – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.
US lawmakers have said that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the House select committee on China, as well as the foreign affairs and the intelligence committees. The dates of the appearances, likely to be behind closed doors, have not been confirmed.
On Monday, Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Haung was an executive until she left in 2025, said it is a “legitimate and lawful business”.
In the past three years, the company was one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, the president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.

But the company – which will report on its quarterly earnings on Tuesday – has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

items.title: Yellow weather warnings issued for snow and ice as temperatures plummet
paragraphs: A spell of cold and wintry weather is set to grip northern areas of the UK early this week, bringing the threat of ice and hill snow.
A yellow weather warning for ice is in effect until 10:00 GMT on Monday after Arctic air pushing across the UK on Sunday night caused temperatures to plummet.
Cold health alerts for parts northern England also remain in force from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.

Some snow is forecast over the hills and mountains in the north over the coming days but the wintry chill will be fairly short-lived in the south, where temperatures will rebound to above average by midweek.
Injuries from slips and falls on icy surfaces are possible as well as difficult driving conditions on Monday morning
Monday morning will start on a chilly note for all parts, although the coldest conditions will be across the northern half of the UK.

Whilst temperatures in the south will generally be a few degrees above freezing, northern England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will wake up to a sharp frost with some wintry flurries over the hills.
A Met Office weather warning for ice is in place until 10:00 GMT on Monday for northern and eastern Scotland as well as part of Cumbria, Northumberland and Durham.
In these regions, showers of rain, sleet or hill snow are likely to fall onto sub-zero surfaces, bringing a risk of icy stretches on untreated roads, pavements and cycle paths.
Cold health alerts, issued by the UKHSA, are also in force across north-west England, north-east England, Yorkshire and the Humber until 21:00 GMT on Thursday.
These alerts are only issued in England and are aimed at health and social care professionals.
Though Monday will be dry and bright for many places, wintry showers will affect some eastern parts of England and Scotland, with these falling as sleet or snow over high ground.
Afternoon maximum temperatures will be a chilly 4-8C in most places - a few degrees below the seasonal average.
Later in the day, the next front will approach from the south-west bringing milder air and some heavy and persistent rain.
As this band of rain then moves northwards overnight into Tuesday, a further spell of hill snow may develop.

A yellow weather warning for snow is set to come into effect on Tuesday from midnight until 12:00 GMT, covering the Midlands, north-east and north-west England, Yorkshire and the Humber and parts of south-west Scotland.
Where snow does accumulate, depths of 1-5cm are likely, although some locations above 300-400m could see 5-15cm.
Some roads and railways are likely to be affected, resulting in longer travel times by road, bus and train services. Power cuts are also possible.
Further south, Tuesday will be a very different day with blustery conditions and some heavy showers.
This battleground of colder, drier conditions in the north and milder, wetter weather in the south will continue into the middle of the week.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

items.title: Tourette's film I Swear wins three Scottish Baftas
paragraphs: I Swear's director, Kirk Jones, thanked the town of Galashiels and Tourette's groups in Scotland for supporting the film as he picked up the first of three awards.
He also paid tribute to John Davidson for sharing his story.

"I know it's been a long and difficult journey," he said. "Thank you for having the strength to continue that journey and for stressing the importance of acceptance and empathy at a time when the world desperately needs it."
He added: "My big hope was that it would help people understand those with Tourette's.

"What I didn't realise was that there's a much wider community of people with neurodiverse conditions who have connected with the film and feel for the first time there's a representation of a condition which is often hidden."
For Davidson, Sunday's wins are the celebration he was hoping for at the Baftas earlier this year.
"Tonight's not really about me, although it is my story," he said.
"It's about celebrating the actors and a beautiful film. I was blown away when I first saw it. I've never watched it since because it makes me cry.
"So I'm chuffed to bits that it's won tonight."
Outlander, which concluded earlier this year after 12 years and eight seasons, won the Outstanding Contribution to Television award.
Culture Secretary Mairi McAllan, who presented the award, said the show had "changed Scotland forever".

She said the Outlander effect had "transformed screen tourism to Scotland, encouraging people to follow in the footsteps of Jamie and Claire, exploring our landscapes, our castles, towns and villages hoping themselves to fall through the stones and into the arms of an 18th Century Highlander".
Accepting the award alongside his fellow stars, Outlander actor Sam Heughan said it was "hard to put into words the impact the show has had".
Bafta Scotland said Outlander also had an "undeniable" impact on Scotland's screen industry, providing opportunities for local talent to develop and flourish.
The Traitors star Stephen Libby, who comes from the Isle of Lewis, won the Audience Award for Favourite On Screen Scot.
The cyber security consultant thanked his parents for letting him be himself, and his partner for his support.
Libby also thanked the BBC and The Traitors for giving him "the opportunity of a lifetime to be on the craziest show".

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
paragraphs: Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out.

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

The laptop’s solid aluminium body, look and feel are identical to its predecessors, using the design first introduced in 2021. With five generations of the machine having been and gone, it is a bit of a known quantity, but the 120Hz miniLED screen is still brilliant, as are the first-class keyboard and trackpad. The port selection is also solid and the MagSafe charging cable remains a delight.

The M6 model only comes with the smaller 14.2in screen, which is still the sweet spot for portability and productivity. It reaches a sustained 1,000nits brightness for standard content and working – double that of the MacBook Air – and hits 1,600nits to make HDR content pop. It is only really beaten by the OLED screen on the new MacBook Pro design, which costs considerably more.
Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones

The M6 is Apple’s latest generation chip and was first used in the Mac mini to great effect. Compared with the M5 generation of chips, including the current MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro is about 11% faster for day-to-day usage and 24% for more intensive multi-core tasks. The extra performance wasn’t that noticeable in day-to-day tasks, but just like the M5 version, it absolutely flies during use.

However, it also has up to 57% faster graphics performance, beating many of Apple’s older M-Pro chips. That makes the M6 quite a leap from older machines with more than enough power for many creative work tasks.

The MacBook Pro also has fantastic battery life, lasting about three days of light work between charges using the browser, messaging, notes and word processing apps. That makes it one of the longest-lasting laptops for general use, but even for more intensive work, developing and editing photos, the battery still lasted about two days.

The MacBook Pro is made of 45% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro M6 costs from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199).

For comparison, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 14in OLED MacBook Pro costs from £2,899, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a potent machine for general use that is let down by its high price, mostly thanks to the scourge of RAMageddon.
But it is also likely one of the last iterations of its design, having been superseded by the new thinner, lighter and OLED-equipped MacBook Pro.
The M6 is a great laptop with fantastically long battery life and a quality screen, keyboard and trackpad, built on the foundations of the many great MacBook Pros over the last five years.

But at £1,999 or equivalent it is also a difficult pill to swallow, primarily aimed at Apple buyers who want a nicer screen or more ports than a MacBook Air and are prepared to pay £700 more for it. For everyone else, there are better models available with more grunt or a cheaper price.

Pros: great performance from M6 chip, minimum of 16GB memory and 1TB storage, super-long battery life, great ProMotion screen, great Centre Stage camera, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, great speakers, Touch ID, top-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, very expensive, not a big upgrade on M5 version, no OLED screen, heavier than newer design.

items.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney
paragraphs: A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.
The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.
The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.
Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.
Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.
Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.
But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.

items.title: Gas starts flowing from Jackdaw after government green light
paragraphs: The Jackdaw platform is located 150 miles east of Aberdeen
Gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field, with the UK energy secretary saying it will help to heat millions of homes and businesses this winter.
Ministers last month announced the Jackdaw field, which lies 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved after years of uncertainty and a court case.
It has now been announced that it has begun producing gas which will start flowing into Britain, according to its operator Adura.
The UK government approved production from the gas field in the North Sea last month, amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Jackdaw is operated by Adura under a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Last month, I gave Jackdaw the green light and today its gas will start flowing into Britain, thanks to the hard work of the skilled North Sea workers.
"It means homegrown gas from this project will help to heat millions of British homes and businesses this winter and beyond, in a boost for our energy security.
"It also will help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission gas as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear."
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at Adura, said the gas field was "now helping to power Britain".

She added: "At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions.
"Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities."
Mueller said the decision was a "positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea".
She added that Adura was "proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades".
Why is the Jackdaw gas field approval so controversial?
Adura has said Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
The decision to green-light Jackdaw drew criticism from some Labour backbenchers and environmentalists, while Conservatives called on the government to also approve the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved for development by the previous Tory government in 2022 and 2023 respectively but these decisions were struck down by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.
This followed a Supreme Court ruling that developers had to account for the climate impact caused by burning fossil fuels in their planning applications.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to stick to the UK's net zero target despite giving the green light to Jackdaw.
He previously said the decision would "significantly strengthen our energy security by increasing domestic gas production by about 6% and support the UK's energy supply for more than a decade".
A decision on the larger Rosebank oil project is yet to be made.
Protesters gathered outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero in Westminster on Wednesday morning
The co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the Jackdaw approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw's operators said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully.
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.

The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
An inside look at Jackdaw, the UK’s newest and most contested gas platform.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.

In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined, external.

"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

items.title: Women pay to break things – level 1
paragraphs: Many women in the UK are visiting new places called rage rooms. In these rooms, people use hammers to break old TVs, plates, and boxes.

People go there because they feel very stressed, tired, or sad about life and work. Owners of these rooms say that most of their visitors are women. Doctors say that it is good to let out bad feelings in a safe space. Men can get angry during sports, but women must be quiet and calm.
Breaking things makes people feel happy and strong for a short time. But it cannot solve big life problems forever.
Difficult words: hammer (a hand tool which we use for breaking things), stressed (worried and upset), owner (a person who has something and it belongs to him or her).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
News in Levels is designed to teach you 3000 words in English. Please follow the instructions below.

items.title: Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office
paragraphs: Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.
Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.
The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.
Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

The tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

“Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” said Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.
“The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.
“The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”

The Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.
Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.
To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

“Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

“This approach was particularly important in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”
He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.
“Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” said Holland.

Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

“As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” said Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”
“In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the company’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.
Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

items.title: Investors sue chip giant Intel after 29% stock plunge
paragraphs: Shareholders have sued US chip giant Intel, accusing it of hiding the severity of a slump in personal computer (PC) sales, which they say led to a nearly 29% one-day collapse in the firm's stock.

A proposed class action lawsuit in San Jose, California said Intel was too late to alert shareholders about how slowing sales could impact its earnings, allegedly artificially inflating its stock price.
Intel shares plunged on 30 October, erasing tens of billions of dollars off its market value the day after it forecasted disappointing revenue in its coming earnings report.

The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders.
Intel has been accused of making "materially false and/or misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, the complaint said.

In October, the firm announced that its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September. That report undermined earlier suggestions from Intel that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit said the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings – a drop of 9%, or about $800m, to $8.1bn.
Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power.
As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive.
Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs.
"We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October.
Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though the stock is still up by 51% overall this year.

items.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since he was jailed.
On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.
HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.
It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.
Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.
In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.
The couple had continued their YouTube podcast during Brand's trial. They often read snippets of the Bible and discussed religion.
On Sunday, Laura told their followers: "We trust his [God's] plan and everything he is doing just now, even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to."
During the show, Laura played an episode she said had been recorded before her husband was jailed.
It featured the couple singing to the American folk singer Woody Guthrie before praying together.
Towards the end of the podcast, Laura returned on her own to read a message from her husband, in which he said he was not guilty for the offences he had been jailed for.
He called staff at HMP Littlehey "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and he asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

items.title: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.

Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

items.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
paragraphs: The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.

As Guardian Australia reported in September, Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

New documents, released under freedom of information requests, reveal the extent to which at least 10 government agencies share sensitive data with the taskforce, which could be fed into Palantir’s software.

The controversial US tech company, co-founded by the Donald Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel, has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that use the software to analyse vast amounts of data.

While the company has insisted it has no access to the data clients enter into the software, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has led calls for a ban on Palantir contracts with the Australian government.

In April, the company implied some cultures were inferior to others in a 22-point manifesto posted on X and described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Shoebridge has said Palantir should not be near Australian data given how the data mining software is used by the IDF and ICE.
The Australian government has spent nearly $80m on Palantir contracts since May.

The taskforce is headed up by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. The intelligence program – known as the fraud fusion centre – is led by the ACIC, and brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce work, according to the documents released under FoI.

The FoI requests, undertaken by Dr Gabrielle Josling, an independent researcher and data scientist, showed at least 10 federal agencies were sharing data with the ACIC – data that could ultimately be put in Palantir’s software by the commission.
Documents from the Department of Education show the ACIC is “collecting criminal intelligence and analysing and crossmatching data” from sources including:
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic).
The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre.
The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations.

The personal information authorised by Services Australia to be obtained by the ACIC includes names, date of birth, information about proof of ID, addresses, telephone numbers, Centrelink claims or reviews, itemised income and asset details, employer information, bank account information and “surveillance material” held by the agency.

The collected data is held by the fraud fusion centre and, while a privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act, the agency’s protocols state it acts in accordance with the Australian privacy principles “wherever reasonably consistent with the effective performance of its statutory functions”.

Services Australia said each disclosure to the ACIC was considered on a case-by-case basis. There had been two disclosures in the financial year to date, compared with 21 in 2025-26 and 47 in 2024-25.

The ATO’s documents do not reveal the extent of the data provided by the agency but state that tax file numbers cannot be provided under law. It made 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026, including 376 to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC.

A spokesperson for the ATO told Guardian Australia the taxpayer information was disclosed where it was “lawfully able” to do so under the terms of the memorandum of understanding as part of the taskforce, the ATO’s intelligence disclosure governance plan and the Tax Administration Act.
The federal education department has withheld releasing information about what data it has provided to the taskforce but the documents state it is data related to the childcare subsidy scheme.
A spokesperson for the department refused to comment on “detailed operational information-sharing arrangements” and directed questions about Palantir use to the ACIC.

The ACIC said data handling is subject to agreements with the agency supplying the data, and that Palantir was “part of a suite of analytical tools to undertake analysis on specific cases to assist partner agencies to disrupt serious organised crime networks defrauding government programs”.

The agency did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia on whether other federal agencies were informed if the data provided was ingested into Palantir’s software. Neither the ATO nor Centrelink were aware if Palantir was used.
“The use of software by another agency is a question for that agency, and any questions relating to ACIC use of data obtained under the FFT are best directed to the ACIC,” an ATO spokesperson said.

The documents reveal that the memorandum of understanding in 2024 between taskforce agencies originally required the taskforce to develop an ethics and human oversight framework governing the control of the information shared. It was described as “an important part of effective risk management for the FFT”.
Ethical risks were supposed to be assessed and recorded on a risks register.

But correspondence released from September 2025 reveals that it was determined that the process was “too difficult to implement” and the framework instead became an “ethics guide” in October last year.

In a submission to the Australian National Audit Office’s review into the taskforce, Josling said the new model abandoned requirements for defined assessments and reviews of the taskforce. A framework for evaluating and monitoring the performance of the taskforce was also not developed.

“A multi-agency taskforce needs a way to learn from data quality problems, data matching limitations, unproductive referrals, emerging risks, and weaknesses in governance,” Josling said in the submission.

Companies and governments have faced pressure to stop using Palantir, with both Coles and Westpac reportedly deciding against renewing their contracts with the firm. The UK government has also faced pressure to drop its contracts with Palantir, including a contract with the NHS.

Palantir has maintained that it does not have access to the data clients enter into its software. A spokesperson has previously defended the company’s contracts with the Australian government, saying it is just a software company.
“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud,” they said.

items.title: Art psychotherapists are already regulated | Letters
paragraphs: We welcome the discussion about public protection, professional accountability and the importance of appropriate regulation within counselling and psychotherapy (Letters, 5 November). However, we feel it is important to highlight a distinction that may be helpful to readers.

Art psychotherapists are already a statutorily regulated profession in the UK, regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC). The HCPC regulates 15 health and care professions, including arts therapists (art psychotherapists, art therapists, drama therapists, music therapists) and the titles art therapist and art psychotherapist are legally protected. Practitioners must meet HCPC registration requirements, standards of proficiency, conduct and ethics, and continuing professional development requirements.
This means that art therapists occupy a different regulatory position from counsellors and psychotherapists, whose professional registration is currently voluntary.

We do recognise the importance of extending statutory protection across professions where it is currently absent, but would appreciate recognition that we, along with drama therapists and music therapists, are a statutory regulated profession. Elizabeth Donnelly Chief executive officer, British Association of Art Therapists

items.title: Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe
paragraphs: Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.
The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.
The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.
In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.
Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.
Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.
For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.
“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”
An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.
All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.
This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.
The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.
According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.
Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.
Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

items.title: With up to $300 off, these early MacBook Black Friday deals might be as good as they're going to get
paragraphs: MacBook Black Friday deals couldn't come soon enough this year following the price hikes amid the ongoing component shortage. Happily, the deals are starting to arrive across major retailers, and some of them may already be as good as they're going to get.
The highlights are $200 off the 2026 M5 MacBook Airs at Amazon, while B&H Photo has up to $300 off M5 MacBook Pros.

Could we still see a discount on the brand-new touchscreen PROLED XDR MacBook Pro released this month? It's unlikely, but perhaps a very small one. If it does come up, you'll find it here because we'll be updating the MacBook deals below throughout Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
If you want to shop around rival brands, see our guide to the best laptops for graphic design. And see our iPad Black Friday hub if you're also after an Apple tablet.

MacBook Black Friday deals in previous years have typically ranged from around $200 MacBook Airs to around $300 off MacBook Pros. Higher-configuration MacBook Pros with 2TB SSDs and 36GB+ memory sometimes come in for bigger discounts of up to around $500, particularly on previous-gen models.

Black Friday 2026 takes place amid a slightly different context compared to previous years because of the shortage of components provoked by the boom in AI data centre construction. Apple hiked the starting price of all MacBooks in mid-2026 because of the component crunch, and prices are unlikely to come back down soon. That may also mean that there's less appetite for discounting during the sale season.

Refurbished MacBooks from reputable sellers like Back Market or Apple's own refurbishment programme can offer exceptional value, especially when you're seeing savings of over $800 / £800. These devices are thoroughly tested, come with warranties, and often include replaced batteries and outer shells, so they look and perform like new.

The main consideration is which generation you're buying – an M1 MacBook from 2020 is still perfectly capable for many people's needs, but it won't support all the latest Apple Intelligence features or handle some heavier creative workflows in video or 3D art. We'd recommend refurbished options if you're primarily using your MacBook for web browsing, productivity apps, and light creative work. However, if you need cutting-edge performance or plan to keep the laptop for five or more years, buying new might be the better long-term investment.

The main differences come down to performance, display technology, and connectivity. MacBook Airs are thinner, lighter and fanless, making them silent and incredibly portable, whilst still offering excellent performance for most users. That makes them ideal for students, writers, and casual users who prioritise battery life and portability.

MacBook Pro models feature more powerful chip configurations (like the M5 Pro and M5 Max), active cooling that allows sustained high performance, brighter displays with ProMotion technology, and additional ports including HDMI and SD card slots. They're designed for professionals doing demanding work like 4K video editing, 3D rendering, or software development.

For most people, a MacBook Air provides more than enough power, but if you're regularly pushing your laptop to its limits with intensive creative or technical work, the MacBook Pro's extra capabilities justify the higher price.

items.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left Megaspeed in 2025, company says
paragraphs: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

items.title: I trusted Adobe Firefly because it was the safe AI option, now I'm not so sure
paragraphs: Adobe spent years selling Firefly on one big reassurance: it was trained on licensed and public-domain content, so you didn't have to worry about where the pixels came from. While other AI companies faced accusations of scraping first and asking questions later, Adobe didn't, and made sure we knew about it. I like that about Firefly and Adobe's push for labelling and clarity, but things are changing.

At MAX this week, Firefly got some noisy neighbours. Models from ByteDance, Google, Kling, OpenAI and ElevenLabs now sit alongside Firefly, with Adobe's Creative Agent in the same place. The keynote line was that creators get to choose, which sounds like a way of passing the buck onto us, the users.

Fine. But I'd like to know what "commercially safe" covers once you've picked someone else's model. The clean-data claim was about Firefly, and I guess it still is, but Firefly now sits alongside less open AI models. Adobe's position with Firefly was never a claim about OpenAI's training set or ByteDance's. A designer or artist clicking through the options could be forgiven for assuming the Adobe badge applies to everything inside the Adobe app. Adobe spells out the distinction in its partner-model documentation, but I'd argue this needs to be much clearer at the point of generation, not buried in the small print.

There's an important distinction here, too: Adobe's commercial-use assurances for its own Firefly models shouldn't be taken as a blanket guarantee for everything generated inside Firefly. Partner models have their own terms, training histories and conditions of use, and users need to assess those separately. For agencies and studios, that difference matters. A Firefly badge isn't necessarily the same as a Firefly guarantee.

Even before opening its gated community to other AI models, Adobe came under pressure from people uploading AI versions of other artists' work and claiming them as Adobe Stock, so some bad actors found ways around Adobe's walled garden. Adobe took action and says it respects creators' rights, and that resemblance isn't proof of copying.

Still, the complaints point at something licensing can't settle. Licensed training data answers whether Adobe was allowed to use the images. Artists were asking whether the output leans on their look. Those are separate questions, and the marketing has tended to let the first stand in for the second.

Add other companies' models and the problem grows. 'Safe' stops describing the product and starts describing one entry on a list. Agencies and art directors who signed off on Firefly because of that word now have to check each model separately, and I suspect most won't. It's this idea that we, the users, the artists and designers, are now responsible for ensuring Firefly outputs are as ethical as they can be.

What I'd want from Adobe is, frankly, very dull and specific. Say in plain language, next to each model, what it was trained on. Say what the safe label does and doesn't cover, style included. Make it easy for studios to lock their workspaces to Firefly models alone, and make those controls available to everyone who needs them.

Adobe has earned a fairly good reputation for adopting AI carefully and responsibly in AI's gold-rush free-for-all. It can keep that and run a marketplace, but only by showing which parts of the marketplace are ethical, carefully made and sourced.

To see what's likely coming down the line, read our report on the Adobe Sneaks from Max 2026, including one in particular that caught the eye: Project Link Up, which is set to make vector design more accessible.

items.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
paragraphs: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

items.title: "The Amiga was my first school": why this pixel artist went back to the computer that made him
paragraphs: “The Amiga was my first school.” For pixel artist Klas Benjaminsson, that’s less nostalgia than a CV. The Swedish creator of the Masters of Pixel Art book series learned his craft on Commodore’s 16-bit wonder, and three decades later, he’s gone back to class, creating a brand-new artwork entirely on an original Amiga 1200 (the Amiga ranks in our best retro consoles guide).

The result is Beyond the Screen: wildlife, lush vegetation and ocean life bursting out of a glowing monitor. It’s built from just 640 x 512 pixels and 32 colours, a canvas that would make a modern phone wallpaper blush. Benjaminsson first sketched in pencil, then brought it to life in Deluxe Paint 4. He calls the Amiga’s limits a “sweet spot”: tight enough to push against, generous enough to make something great.
It’s also a nod to Jim Sachs’ Amiga Lagoon, the picture that showed a generation what these machines could do, and a love letter to an era when your imagination really was the only limit.

The timing is no accident. Retro Games’ full-size Amiga 1200 replica, THEA1200, lands on 4 December. Unlike the A500 Mini we reviewed in 2022, it comes with a working keyboard and Workbench desktop, so it’s built for creating as well as playing.

Artists can join in too, with PosterSpy inviting its community to reimagine Benjaminsson’s piece in their own style. Need a pixel fix first? Dive into our 31 amazing pixel art examples or learn how to break into pixel art. Then read on as Benjaminsson explains why limits still make for better art, and which retro tools you should try first.
The new THEA1200 arrives on 4 December. See more of Klas Benjaminsson's poster art at PosterSpy x THEA1200.
Klas Benjaminsson: One key point in the initiative of THEA1200 is to recreate the Amiga 1200 in modern shape, so it made sense to honor the original platform.

KB: To be honest, the work "Amiga Lagoon" by Jim Sachs was a very important piece from the beginning. It visualised the power and creativity of the Amiga, and we agreed that an indirect homage to this masterpiece would be suitable for this occasion.There was an idea to create a “flow” coming out from the screen, showing waves of animals, nature and wildlife - flowing and growing out from this creative computer. I wanted a feeling that communicated “only your imagination sets the limits”.From sketch to finish, animals changed and shifted positions. But I felt the core idea was good and continued the work until the end.

KB: For me personally, growing up with the Amiga 500 and 1200 graphic standards, these limitations became something of a sweet spot for me. Limited enough to make it interesting to push the borders on what could be done, but also good enough to make it possible to create some great designs.
KB: Deluxe Paint 4 on the Amiga was where bulk of work was done. Photoshop and GrafX2 on the PC: importing the sketches and converting formats for export.

KB: To be honest I think many of modern pixel artists are doing a great job. There are hundreds of active pixel artists right now, posting pixel art on a daily basis with no direct platform or set rules for limits in their work space, but they still set a limited palette and a certain pixel area for their work. I think it's an awesome homage to the old platforms, which lives on so vividly in these modern pixel art works even today.

KB: Digital graphics had a big impact in my youth. As a kid I enjoyed playing video games, but as a young aspiring “artist” I also studied the graphics of the many games I tried (both Arcade and on my own C64). It took several years until a friend of mine showed me his brand new Amiga 500 with Deluxe Paint – that was the moment I realised I might be able to create something like that myself.I took the first steps on a very long and interesting journey on finally becoming an art director. The Amiga was my first school that defined much of my professional life.

KB: There are many techniques that more or less could be described as artistic knowledge, which I learned on the Amiga but aren't unique for this medium/platform. But there are some routines that could be blamed on my background with old-school pixel art:- The importance of setting a palette early on in the design process.- To keep full control of the pixels and resolution.

KB: The Amiga provides an interesting set of limitations to work with if you are into pixel art. Enforcing a specific resolution and a limited colour palette when creating pixel art is a very challenging and demanding practice, which forces the artist to be precise. With these clear restrictions in place, much more focus can be aimed at the actual creative work instead.

KB: I personally find it fascinating to take photos with a classic analogue camera, and see how the film can change with exposure settings. It's a special and rewarding experience to go through the processes by hand. You try and learn by mistakes, testing ideas, creating and discarding concepts, and finally finding a way to express your ideas. Digital tools can be a great help, working alongside you when sketching and trying out ideas. But there is a certain magic about when doing it by yourself, learning the craft.

KB: If you are into pixel art, don't hesitate to try out Deluxe Paint or Brilliance! These are the original software from which most modern pixel art tools has taken their UI concepts, as well as the early versions of Photoshop.If you are into creating music, try out some of the tracker software such as ProTracker, or AHX for unique chip sounds.For young people learning to code, AMOS is a fun and powerful language to start with. Something that could transition into C++ later on.Another nice tool was Dir Opus, file-handling made easy and logical. I wish Microsoft or Apple would have picked it up back in the days....

items.title: Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico
paragraphs: A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.
Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.
“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.
“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”
Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.
It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.
Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.
Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

Rosadoce’s distinct front elevation is formed from a series of staggered openings, described by the studio as evoking an “inverted stair”. This allows in light and ventilation while maintaining privacy.
“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.
“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.
This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.
According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.
“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.
The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.
Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

items.title: Mecanoo transforms former gold vault into "city’s living room" in renovation of De Nederlandsche Bank in Amsterdam
paragraphs: Dutch firm Mecanoo has completed a major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank, which involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault.
The Francine Houben-led architecture studio oversaw a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.
Located in the heart of Amsterdam, this huge concrete-slab building is in complete contrast to the city’s historic canal houses.

The original architect, Marius Frans Duintjer, had hoped to emulate the modernist works of Mies van der Rohe, but security requirements had resulted in “a fortress with fences, large boulders and armed military police,” according to Mecanoo.
The building was further complicated by later extensions, which included an extra storey above the low-rise main building and a cylindrical 14-storey tower built alongside the original central tower.
Mecanoo’s transformation was enabled by the relocation of gold reserves and banknote operations to a location in Zeist.
This allowed the architects to give the building a sense of transparency and openness that was envisioned from the outset, but had never been possible before now.
The project is an exemplar for sustainable renovation, as proven by its nomination for Dezeen Awards 2026.
Removing the cylindrical tower was pivotal, as it allowed space for a new public garden at the heart of the scheme.
This tower was carefully dismantled, allowing many materials to be reused.
Salvaged concrete was used to build a new quay beside the canal, while the rest was donated to social housing projects in the city.
The removal enabled a reorganisation of the ground floor.
The entrance was relocated to Frederiksplein, while floorplates were cut away to reveal the 61-metre-long former vault, which has been transformed into an exhibition gallery.
“The most secretive part of the bank is now its most public,” said Mecanoo.
“Inside the vault, visitors can immerse themselves in exhibitions and interactive games that tell the story of gold, money, the economy and DNB’s core activities.”
The retained structures were newly clad in red ceramic bricks. These incorporate the brown tiles that clad the building previously, with the old tiles crushed for use as pigment.

These combine with new glazing, a Kastenfenster system of ventilated double-glazing with integrated sun shading, which has helped to reduce the building’s day-to-day energy requirements by an estimated 80 per cent.
Inside, the space linking the vault with the courtyard was designed as an indoor street, with seating areas along the edges and auditoriums (one formal, the other informal) at each end.
“Francine Houben’s inspiration came from the vibrant ‘street’ of the central hall in the former Faculty of Architecture building at TU Delft, which was destroyed by fire,” said Mecanoo.
The rest of the building is organised into zones with varying levels of security.

A five-storey atrium organises the semi-public area, which includes a meeting centre and a restaurant overlooking the Singelgracht, while the more secure employee zones are located in both the courtyard building and the tower.
The meeting centre occupies what was previously a double-height cash hall, with distinctive tree-like columns.
The original spiral staircase still stands, alongside a second added by Mecanoo, while custom-designed tables feature integrated lamps.
Timber was used for many of the new surfaces, including a slatted ceiling made from locally felled poplar trees.
Shades of red, blue and orange extend across other surfaces and interior elements, including walls covered in recycled-plastic felt, carpets and furniture.
“The colour scheme is inspired by the vibrant paper currency from the last period of the Dutch guilder,” said Mecanoo.
The interiors are completed by DNB’s collection of artwork, energy-efficient lighting systems and circular planting boxes.

“The renovation transforms De Nederlandsche Bank from a closed fortress into a transparent circular landmark, repurposing the former gold vault as the city’s living room for the public,” concluded Mecanoo.
Other recent projects by the firm include the rock-like Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, the tile-clad Villa BW and the book-inspired Macau Central Library.

items.title: The Tesla Cybercab sounds like the ultimate subscription trap
paragraphs: Just days after we were passing our last respects to the Cybertruck, the Tesla Cybercab is finally available to order. Alas, like with the "flying Roadster", there's some important small print.

The Cybercab will initially only be usable in the same locations where Tesla's Robotaxi ride-hailing service operates, which means it will be geofenced to specific parts of Texas and Florida. Even then, to use it at all, customers will have to pay a hefty monthly subscription fee on top of the upfront cost. Cancel the subscription, and you've got an expensive decoration sitting in your driveway.
If you thought Adobe's subscription model was bad, at least there's the Creative Cloud Black Friday sale.

Cybercab sales aren't opening to the public at large. Like with the flight-mode Roadster, you'll need a personal invite from Tesla. Nevertheless, the company says it expects to make the first deliveries in Austin, Texas, as soon as December.
Those who get an invite will have to pay $29,990 for the car itself. If they want the vehicle to actually drive, they'll have to also commit to a Tesla Autonomy Subscription at $299 per month.

People generally don't like subscriptions. Companies do since recurring payments usually provide higher margins and more stable long-term revenue than a one-off sale. People willingly accept that approach for phone data, streaming services and software, but it stings a but more when it comes with a physical product that also has an up-front cost.

Other carmakers have been roasted for this. BMW wanted people to pay $18 a month for heated seats. Mercedes-EQ decided to cap performance and ransom it back to customers in the form of an Acceleration Increase costing $100 a month. Other cash graps have included paywalled key fobs and garage door opening.
The Future Has Arrived | Cybercab - YouTube

Admittedly, the Tesla Cybercab is different beast. You could argue that its autonomous driving capability is the real product and that the vehicle is just the shell for it. That service entails plenty of real ongoing costs for cloud infrastructure, remote monitoring systems, maps and safety updates.

The controversial part is that the vehicle's usability will depend on the Autonomy Subscription because it has no manual controls. Cancelling won't downgrade it to a normal car – it makes it unusable. It's a piece of hardware whose usability depends entirely on an ongoing software service controlled by Tesla.
For comparison, an extra $10,000 would get you a Tesla Model Y with manual controls and an optional full-self driving (FSD) subscription at $100 per month.

Even Tesla CEO Elon Musk thinks the Cybercab monthly fee that his company is quoting is "too high". Writing on X in response to a post by YouTuber Marques Brownlee, he suggested that it "should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month."

That might give Cybercab customers hope that the price will come down in the future. But it could also go up. The Tesla Autonomy Subscription Agreement states that the company reserves the right to adjust the monthly fee with just a month's notice. If it hikes the cost beyond a price you're prepared to pay, you lose the use of your car.

@MKBHD It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.November 14, 2026

The agreement also allows Tesla to retain a lot of control over the product you just bought. It can modify service areas, update operating conditions, and control access to autonomous operation remotely. At least initially, those buying the car for personal-use will not be allowed to put it to work on ride-hailing networks. The car also films you during the entire ride and will pull over if the camera detects that you're infringing Tesla's rules.
These are unusual limitations compared with traditional car ownership, making it feel more like a temporary lease of a product whose branding Tesla hasn't yet managed to trademark.

items.title: The stunning Star Wars Lego anniversary poster makes me finally get it
paragraphs: The Star Wars 50th anniversary is approaching, and that's not only a big deal for Disney and Lucasfilm. It's also big for Lego.

I have to admit that I've not really 'got' the Lego Star Wars collaborations so far, but this piece is a real beauty. The anniversary model is a stunning 3,209-piece recreation one of the best Star Wars posters.

I was a massive Lego fan as a a kid, and then two things happened. I grew up, and so did Lego. While I got into other forms of entertainment, Lego got into collaborations, and big time. It still makes some classic sets, but most of its energy is put into partnerships with franchises from Disney and Marvel to Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings and Fortnite.

The extreme was when it started making logo kits for Star Wars and Marvel. I love it that a YouTuber made 100 famous logos out of Lego, but $100 for a dedicated set that lets you build a Lego Marvel logo? It felt like a product who's only use would be as a decoration on a YouTuber or streamer's desk.
But the Lego Star Wars A New Hope poster is something else. With its size and the level of detail, this is a piece you could put on a wall as a piece of interior design, turning Lego into art.

According to Brick Fanatics' interview with model designer Steven Howard, the logo was actually the most difficult part to create. Because of that, the text was made slightly bigger than on the original poster at 32 studs wide for the bottom row of the text.
The Lego A New Hope Movie Poster will cost $299. It's just a shame that it's not coming out until 4 January, otherwise it would be the perfect Christmas gift for any Star Wars fan.
